Certain particles — called "subjunctive installers" — reach into the verb and change that -u to **-a**, and in the plural forms they delete the final ن entirely.

The two installers you'll meet daily:

**أَنْ (an, "to/that")** — after verbs of wanting, ability, intention:

- **أُرِيدُ أَنْ أَذْهَبَ** (urīdu an adhhaba) — "I want to go." (Not *an adhhhabu.)
- **يُمْكِنُ أَنْ نَبْدَأَ** (yumkinu an nabda'a) — "We can begin / it is possible that we begin."

**لَنْ (lan)** — the future negator:

- **لَنْ أَذْهَبَ** (lan adhhaba) — "I will not go."
- **لَنْ يَصِلُوا** (lan yaṣilū) — "They will not arrive." — watch the plural: يَصِلُونَ (yaṣilūna) lost its ن under lan, leaving yaṣilū. That missing ن is the subjunctive's fingerprint in plurals, and in the feminine singular too: لَنْ تَكْتُبِي (lan taktubī, from taktubīna).

Other installers exist — حَتَّى (ḥattā, "until/so that"), كَيْ (kay, "in order to"), لِـ of purpose (li-, "to") — **جِئْتُ لِأَتَعَلَّمَ** (ji'tu li-ataʿallama, "I came to learn") — but an and lan cover most of what a learner reads.

Think of the moods as three costumes for the same verb: **-u for plain statements, -a after the subjunctive particles, and a clipped bare form after the jussive particles** (لَمْ lam — the next costume). The particles are few and fixed; once your ear expects the -a after أنْ and لنْ, you'll hear a missing one as a wrong note — which is exactly how native speakers experience it.
Why does 'he did not go' come out as لم يذهب with the verb looking present-tense and cut short?

Because Arabic negates the past with a time machine. **لَمْ** (lam) takes a present-tense verb, puts it in the **jussive** mood (المجزوم) — clipped ending, no final vowel — and the combination *means* past:

**لَمْ يَذْهَبْ**
lam yadhhab
"He did not go." (Literally: lam + "he-goes" — the lam does the time travel.)

The jussive's marks:

- Singular: the -u of the indicative drops to sukūn: يَذْهَبُ (yadhhabu) → يَذْهَبْ (yadhhab)
- Plurals and the feminine singular: the final ن deletes, as in the subjunctive: يَذْهَبُونَ → **لَمْ يَذْهَبُوا** (lam yadhhabū)
- Hollow verbs shorten their long vowel: يَقُولُ (yaqūlu) → **لَمْ يَقُلْ** (lam yaqul, "he did not say"); يَبِيعُ → **لَمْ يَبِعْ** (lam yabiʿ, "he did not sell")

لَمْ is also the standard way to say "not yet" and to deny flatly: **لَمْ أَفْهَمْ** (lam afham, "I didn't/don't understand") — the sentence learners say most in Arabic class, and a perfectly polite one.

Its partner in the jussive is **لَا** of prohibition: **لَا تَذْهَبْ** (lā tadhhab, "Don't go!") — same clipped verb, different particle, command instead of report.

Now step back and see the mood system whole, because lam completes it:

| Mood | Ending | Trigger | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| Indicative | -u | default | يَكْتُبُ (he writes) |
| Subjunctive | -a | أَنْ، لَنْ | لَنْ يَكْتُبَ (he won't write) |
| Jussive | clipped | لَمْ، لَا (command) | لَمْ يَكْتُبْ (he didn't write) |

Three endings, a handful of particles, and every present-tense verb in the language snaps into the system. The "cut short" look of لم يذهب is not damage — it's the jussive doing exactly its one job.
Verbs like مشى (walked) and دعا (called) end in what looks like a long vowel, and their presents look unrelated — يمشي، يدعو. Help?

These are the **defective verbs** — roots whose *last* letter is weak (و or ي). The weak final letter changes costume between past and present, which is why the two tenses look like strangers.

Two families, distinguished by the present:

**The yamshī family** (root ends in ي):
- **مَشَى** (mashā) — he walked → **يَمْشِي** (yamshī) — he walks
- **جَرَى** (jarā) — he ran → **يَجْرِي** (yajrī)
- **بَكَى** (bakā) — he cried → **يَبْكِي** (yabkī)

**The yadʿū family** (root ends in و):
- **دَعَا** (daʿā) — he called/invited → **يَدْعُو** (yadʿū) — he calls
- **رَجَا** (rajā) — he hoped → **يَرْجُو** (yarjū)

And a third small group keeps its ي visible in the past: **نَسِيَ** (nasiya, "he forgot") → **يَنْسَى** (yansā, "he forgets").

Reading the past spellings: mashā's final **ى** is alif maqṣūra — a ى that sounds ā. That ى is the ي in disguise. In daʿā, the final ا is the و stretched out. The past hides the weak letter as a long vowel; the present reveals it as ي or و. Same trick as the hollow verbs, played at the end of the word instead of the middle.

The suffixes expose everything. Add "I" and the weak letter reappears as ي in both families: **مَشَيْتُ** (mashaytu, "I walked"), **دَعَوْتُ** (daʿawtu, "I called" — here و resurfaces). "She" shortens: **مَشَتْ** (mashat, "she walked"), **دَعَتْ** (daʿat, "she called").

Strategy: when you meet a past-tense verb ending in ا or ى, assume a weak final letter, and let the present tense tell you whether it's a و or a ي verb. Dictionaries file these under the full root — مشى under م ش ي, دعا under د ع و — so this one identification unlocks the entry.
أدرس الأفعال العربية وأجد صعوبة في الأفعال المعتلة مثل «قال» و«باع». كيف أفهمها؟

الأفعال المعتلة هي أفعال فيها حرف علة — واو أو ياء أو ألف — في أولها أو وسطها أو آخرها. أصعبها للمبتدئ ما كان حرف العلة في وسطه، ويسمى **الأجوف**.
(Al-afʿāl al-muʿtalla hiya afʿāl fīhā ḥarf ʿilla — wāw aw yā' aw alif. Aṣʿabuhā mā kāna ḥarf al-ʿilla fī wasaṭihi, wa-yusammā al-ajwaf.)

انظر إلى المثالين:
(Inẓur ilā l-mithālayn:)

- **قَالَ** (qāla — he said): جذره **ق و ل**. في الماضي اختفت الواو وصارت ألفًا طويلة، وفي المضارع تعود: **يَقُولُ** (yaqūlu — he says).
- **بَاعَ** (bāʿa — he sold): جذره **ب ي ع**. في الماضي صارت الياء ألفًا، وفي المضارع تعود ياءً: **يَبِيعُ** (yabīʿu — he sells).

القاعدة الذهبية: **المضارع يكشف سر الماضي**. إذا رأيت «ā» في وسط الماضي، فابحث في المضارع: واوٌ تعود واوًا (يقول)، وياءٌ تعود ياءً (يبيع).
(Al-qāʿida ad-dhahabiyya: al-muḍāriʿ yakshifu sirr al-māḍī.)

أفعال جوفاء مشهورة أخرى:
(Afʿāl jawfā' mashhūra ukhrā:)

- **كَانَ / يَكُونُ** (kāna / yakūnu — to be)
- **نَامَ / يَنَامُ** (nāma / yanāmu — to sleep)
- **زَارَ / يَزُورُ** (zāra / yazūru — to visit)
- **سَارَ / يَسِيرُ** (sāra / yasīru — to walk)

وملاحظة أخيرة: عندما يتصل بالفعل ضمير مثل «تُ»، يقصر الصوت الطويل: **قُلْتُ** (qultu — I said)، **بِعْتُ** (biʿtu — I sold).
(Wa-mulāḥaẓa akhīra: ʿindamā yattaṣilu bi-l-fiʿl ḍamīr mithl "-tu", yaqṣuru ṣ-ṣawt aṭ-ṭawīl: qultu, biʿtu.)

لا تحفظ كل فعل وحده؛ احفظ الجذر والمضارع معًا، وستقرأ العائلة كلها.
(Lā taḥfaẓ kull fiʿl waḥdahu; iḥfaẓ al-jadhr wa-l-muḍāriʿ maʿan.)
Is it true Arabic thinks the sun is female and the moon is male? That seems oddly specific.

True, and it's the best memory hook in Arabic grammar. **الشمس** (ash-shams, "the sun") is feminine; **القمر** (al-qamar, "the moon") is masculine. Every Arabic speaker carries this pair from childhood:

- **الشَّمْسُ سَاخِنَةٌ** (ash-shamsu sākhinatun) — "The sun is hot" — feminine adjective سَاخِنَة.
- **الْقَمَرُ مُنِيرٌ** (al-qamaru munīrun) — "The moon is shining/bright" — masculine adjective مُنِير.

And here's the gift hidden inside the pair: ش is a **sun letter** and ق is a **moon letter**. The two words that name the sun/moon letter rule are themselves the sun and the moon, each demonstrating its own class. الشمس swallows the l of ال (ash-shams); القمر keeps it (al-qamar). Grammar teachers have exploited this coincidence for a thousand years.

The broader truth: every Arabic noun is masculine or feminine, and most of the time you cannot guess from meaning — a sun is not "female" in any conceptual sense, it's grammatically feminine the way French *la lune* is. But the pair teaches the survival skill: **gender is a property of the word, learned with the word**, like its plural.

Some genders do follow meaning (رجل rajul "man" is masculine, امرأة imra'a "woman" is feminine) and most words ending in ة are feminine. The rest — شمس feminine, قمر masculine, باب bāb "door" masculine, سيارة sayyāra "car" feminine by its ة — are vocabulary facts.

Learn nouns the way dictionaries print them, with gender attached, and let الشمس والقمر be your permanent reminder that the system is arbitrary, consistent, and — once you stop fighting it — rather beautiful.
كيف أعرف أن الكلمة مؤنثة؟ هل التاء المربوطة هي العلامة الوحيدة؟

لا، التاء المربوطة هي العلامة الأشهر، لكنها ليست الوحيدة.
(Lā, at-tā' al-marbūṭa hiya al-ʿalāma al-ashhar, lākinnahā laysat al-waḥīda.)

**العلامة الأولى: التاء المربوطة (ة)** في آخر الكلمة: **مدرسة** (madrasa — school)، **سيارة** (sayyāra — car)، **حديقة** (ḥadīqa — garden)، **طالبة** (ṭāliba — female student).
(Al-ʿalāma al-ūlā: at-tā' al-marbūṭa fī ākhir al-kalima.)

**العلامة الثانية: الألف المقصورة أو الممدودة** في آخر أسماء معينة: **ذِكْرَى** (dhikrā — memory)، **صَحْرَاء** (ṣaḥrā' — desert)، **حَمْرَاء** (ḥamrā' — red, feminine).
(Al-ʿalāma ath-thāniya: al-alif al-maqṣūra aw al-mamdūda.)

**لكن انتبه**: توجد كلمات مؤنثة **بلا أي علامة**: **شمس** (shams — sun)، **أرض** (arḍ — earth/land)، **حرب** (ḥarb — war)، **نار** (nār — fire)، **يد** (yad — hand)، **عين** (ʿayn — eye).
(Lākin intabih: tūjadu kalimāt mu'annatha bilā ayy ʿalāma: shams, arḍ, ḥarb, nār, yad, ʿayn.)

وتوجد كلمات **بها التاء المربوطة وهي مذكرة**: **خليفة** (khalīfa — caliph، رجل)، و**علّامة** (ʿallāma — great scholar، رجل أيضًا). التاء هنا جزء من الكلمة لا علامة تأنيث.
(Wa-tūjadu kalimāt bihā t-tā' al-marbūṭa wa-hiya mudhakkara: khalīfa, ʿallāma. At-tā' hunā juz' min al-kalima.)

الطريقة العملية: احفظ كل اسم جديد مع جنسه، واستعمل **هذا / هذه** اختبارًا سريعًا: **هذه الشمس** (hādhihi sh-shams) مؤنثة، و**هذا القمر** (hādhā l-qamar) مذكر.
(Aṭ-ṭarīqa al-ʿamaliyya: iḥfaẓ kull ism jadīd maʿa jinsihi, wa-staʿmil hādhā/hādhihi ikhtibāran sarīʿan.)
Why does 'red' change its whole shape for feminine — أحمر becomes حمراء instead of just adding ة?

Because colors (and many physical descriptors) belong to a special adjective pattern with its own masculine and feminine molds:

- Masculine: **أَفْعَل** (afʿal) — **أَحْمَر** (aḥmar, red), **أَبْيَض** (abyaḍ, white), **أَسْوَد** (aswad, black), **أَزْرَق** (azraq, blue), **أَخْضَر** (akhḍar, green), **أَصْفَر** (aṣfar, yellow)
- Feminine: **فَعْلَاء** (faʿlā') — **حَمْرَاء** (ḥamrā'), **بَيْضَاء** (bayḍā'), **سَوْدَاء** (sawdā'), **زَرْقَاء** (zarqā'), **خَضْرَاء** (khaḍrā'), **صَفْرَاء** (ṣafrā')

So: **قَمِيصٌ أَحْمَرُ** (qamīṣun aḥmaru, "a red shirt" — shirt is masculine) but **سَيَّارَةٌ حَمْرَاءُ** (sayyāratun ḥamrā'u, "a red car" — car is feminine). No ة anywhere; the whole mold changes.

This afʿal/faʿlā' pair is bigger than colors. It's also the mold of the **elative** — the comparative/superlative: **أَكْبَر** (akbar, "bigger/biggest") from كبير, **أَجْمَل** (ajmal, "more beautiful"), **أَوَّل** (awwal, "first"). Same أَفْعَل skeleton, different job — context and construction separate them (a color afʿal describes; an elative afʿal compares or ranks).

Two more facts for your notebook:

1. **The plural of color adjectives** is فُعْل (fuʿl): حُمْر (ḥumr, red ones), بِيض (bīḍ, white ones) — you'll meet it in literary descriptions: **خَيْلٌ حُمْرٌ** (khaylun ḥumrun, "red horses").
2. **In dialects**, the feminine color often gets regularized — Egyptians say حمرا (ḥamra) for feminine red, a shortened faʿlā' — and in casual speech many just use the masculine form for everything. MSA keeps the full pair, and written Arabic expects it.

Learn colors as pairs from the start — aḥmar/ḥamrā', abyaḍ/bayḍā' — the way you learn nouns with their plurals. The mold is strange once and automatic forever after.
How does verb agreement work with groups — 'the girls went', 'the boys went'? My book shows ذهبن and ذهبوا.

Arabic verbs agree with their subject in gender and number, and the past tense shows it most clearly because every person has its own suffix. Using ذَهَبَ (dhahaba, "to go"):

- **ذَهَبَ الْوَلَدُ** (dhahaba l-waladu) — the boy went (masc. sg. — the bare stem)
- **ذَهَبَتِ الْبِنْتُ** (dhahabati l-bintu) — the girl went (-at, feminine sg.)
- **ذَهَبَ الْأَوْلَادُ** in verb-first order — but the full-agreement form you asked about is subject-first: **الْأَوْلَادُ ذَهَبُوا** (al-awlādu dhahabū) — the boys went (-ū)
- **الْبَنَاتُ ذَهَبْنَ** (al-banātu dhahabna) — the girls went (-na)

The two plural endings are a minimal pair worth burning in: **ـُوا (-ū)** masculine, **ـْنَ (-na)** feminine. They recur in the present tense as well: يَذْهَبُونَ (yadhhabūna) / يَذْهَبْنَ (yadhhabna).

Now the subtlety you may remember from the word-order lesson: when the verb comes **first**, it wears a singular form even before a plural subject — **ذَهَبَ الْأَوْلَادُ** (dhahaba l-awlādu, verb masc. sg.) and **ذَهَبَتِ الْبَنَاتُ** (dhahabati l-banātu, verb fem. sg.). Gender always agrees; number agrees fully only when the subject leads.

Gender agreement also outranks common sense in one direction: a mixed group — boys and girls together — takes the **masculine** plural by grammatical convention: الطلاب (aṭ-ṭullāb) covers a mixed class, and **الطلاب ذهبوا** uses -ū. This is a grammar rule, stated as grammar; the feminine plural is for groups that are entirely female.

Practical drill: take any verb and run the quartet — walad, bint, awlād (subject-first), banāt (subject-first) — until the four endings come out without thought. Agreement errors are the most common learner errors in Arabic, and also the most forgiven: nobody misunderstands ذهب البنات with a masculine verb; they just hear a student. Precision here is polish, not survival.
Can we revisit the rule about things-plurals taking feminine singular agreement? I want more examples in full sentences.

Let's give the rule a full workout. The principle: **a plural of non-human things is grammatically treated as one feminine singular unit** — demonstrative, adjective, and verb all go feminine singular.

**Demonstratives:**
- **هَذِهِ الْكُتُبُ جَدِيدَةٌ** (hādhihi l-kutubu jadīdatun) — "These books are new." هذه is "this (f.)" — used for a shelf of books.
- **تِلْكَ السَّيَّارَاتُ غَالِيَةٌ** (tilka s-sayyārātu ghāliyatun) — "Those cars are expensive."

**Adjectives:**
- **الْأَبْوَابُ مَفْتُوحَةٌ** (al-abwābu maftūḥatun) — "The doors are open."
- **الْأَسْئِلَةُ صَعْبَةٌ** (al-as'ilatu ṣaʿbatun) — "The questions are hard." (أسئلة is the broken plural of سؤال, masculine — still feminine singular agreement.)
- **أَيَّامٌ بَارِدَةٌ** (ayyāmun bāridatun) — "cold days."

**Verbs:**
- **وَصَلَتِ الرَّسَائِلُ** (waṣalati r-rasā'ilu) — "The letters/messages arrived." Feminine singular verb وَصَلَتْ before a plural of things.
- **انْكَسَرَتِ الْكَرَاسِيُّ** (inkasarati l-karāsiyyu) — "The chairs broke." One -t, plural chairs.

**The contrast, humans:**
- **وَصَلَ الْمُهَنْدِسُونَ** (waṣala l-muhandisūna) — "The engineers arrived" (masc. verb form, plural subject — and subject-first: الْمُهَنْدِسُونَ وَصَلُوا with full plural verb).
- **الرَّسَائِلُ وَصَلَتْ / الْمُهَنْدِسُونَ وَصَلُوا** — messages: fem. sg. verb; engineers: masc. pl. verb. Same verb, two agreements, decided entirely by whether the subject is people.

Edge cases to know honestly: plurals of animals usually follow the things-rule (الكلاب كبيرة, "the dogs are big" — fem. sg.), though elevated style sometimes treats them as rational. And a *sound* feminine plural of things behaves identically: السياراتُ واقفةٌ (as-sayyārātu wāqifatun, "the cars are parked").

One sentence to carry: **things gather into a "she," people stay a "they."** Every agreement puzzle with a non-human plural dissolves once you hear it that way.
Give me a reference table for Arabic demonstratives — this, that, these, those.

Demonstratives (أسماء الإشارة) — Arabic demonstratives agree in gender and number with what they point at, and they split near (**this**) from far (**that**). The pointing word usually comes *before* the noun, which then takes ال: هذا الكتاب (hādhā l-kitāb, "this book").

| | Near — "this/these" | Far — "that/those" |
|---|---|---|
| masc. sg. | **هَذَا** (hādhā) | **ذَلِكَ** (dhālika) |
| fem. sg. | **هَذِهِ** (hādhihi) | **تِلْكَ** (tilka) |
| masc. dual | **هَذَانِ** (hādhāni) | **ذَانِكَ** (dhānika) |
| fem. dual | **هَاتَانِ** (hātāni) | **تَانِكَ** (tānika) |
| plural (people) | **هَؤُلَاءِ** (hā'ulā'i) | **أُولَئِكَ** (ulā'ika) |
| plural (things) | **هَذِهِ** (hādhihi) | **تِلْكَ** (tilka) |

In use:

- **هَذَا بَيْتِي** (hādhā baytī) — "This is my house." (Sentence: demonstrative + noun = "this is…")
- **هَذِهِ سَيَّارَتِي** (hādhihi sayyāratī) — "This is my car."
- **هَؤُلَاءِ طُلَّابِي** (hā'ulā'i ṭullābī) — "These are my students."
- **ذَلِكَ الرَّجُلُ مُعَلِّمِي** (dhālika r-rajulu muʿallimī) — "That man is my teacher."

Three notes that save confusion:

1. **Things-plurals borrow the feminine singular row** — هذه الكتب (hādhihi l-kutub, "these books"), exactly the non-human plural rule you know from adjectives.
2. **هَؤُلَاءِ is for people** (or beings treated as rational). Pointing at a crowd of men or women: هؤلاء. Pointing at a pile of objects: هذه.
3. **Alone vs. attached**: هَذَا alone means "this is…" in a sentence (هذا بيتي), while هَذَا الْبَيْتُ (hādhā l-baytu) means "this house" as a phrase — the ال on the noun is what turns the sentence into a phrase. In dialects, هذا shrinks: Egyptian **ده** (da, m.) / **دي** (di, f.) / **دول** (dōl, pl.), usually placed *after* the noun: الكتاب ده (il-kitāb da, "this book").
How do I say 'my book', 'your car', 'his house' in Arabic? Are there separate possessive words?

No separate words — Arabic glues possession onto the noun itself with **possessive suffixes**. The noun is the host; the ending is the owner:

Using **كِتَاب** (kitāb, book):

| Owner | Form | Transliteration |
|---|---|---|
| my | كِتَابِي | kitābī |
| your (m.) | كِتَابُكَ | kitābuka |
| your (f.) | كِتَابُكِ | kitābuki |
| his | كِتَابُهُ | kitābuhu |
| her | كِتَابُهَا | kitābuhā |
| our | كِتَابُنَا | kitābunā |
| your (pl.) | كِتَابُكُمْ | kitābukum |
| their | كِتَابُهُمْ | kitābuhum |

So **سَيَّارَتُهُ** (sayyāratuhu) is "his car" — the ة of سيارة turns to ت before a suffix (sayyāra**t**uhu), another tā' marbūṭa sighting — and **بَيْتُهَا** (baytuhā) is "her house," **بَيْتِي** (baytī) "my house."

The same suffixes attach to **prepositions**, giving you the whole "with me / for him / on her" family for free:

- **مَعِي** (maʿī) — with me; **مَعَهُ** (maʿahu) — with him
- **لَهُ** (lahu) — for/to him; **لَهَا** (lahā) — for her
- **عَلَيْهِ** (ʿalayhi) — on him (note: ʿalā's ā becomes ay before suffixes)
- **فِيهِ** (fīhi) — in it/him

And to verbs, where they become **objects**: **أَعْرِفُهُ** (aʿrifuhu, "I know him"), **رَأَيْتُهَا** (ra'aytuhā, "I saw her").

Two usage notes. First, a noun with a possessive suffix is automatically definite — كتابي is "*the* book of mine," "my book," never "a book of mine." Second, dialect trims the vowels (Egyptian kitābu → "kitābo," كتابه pronounced kitābo) but keeps the suffix system intact. Possession in Arabic is not a word you add; it's a tail the noun grows.
Is there any logic to which nouns are feminine? Body parts, maybe?

There is a partial logic, and body parts are its most famous province: **paired body parts are usually feminine.**

- **عَيْن** (ʿayn) — eye: feminine
- **يَد** (yad) — hand: feminine
- **رِجْل** (rijl) — leg/foot: feminine
- **أُذُن** (udhun) — ear: feminine
- **كَتِف** (katif) — shoulder: feminine

against the unpaired or singular organs, often masculine:

- **رَأْس** (ra's) — head: masculine
- **قَلْب** (qalb) — heart: masculine
- **أَنْف** (anf) — nose: masculine
- **فَم** (fam) — mouth: masculine

"Usually" is doing honest work in that sentence — كتف appears as both in classical usage, and إصبع (iṣbaʿ, finger) swings both ways in the dictionaries. But as a first guess for a new paired body part, feminine wins far more often than chance.

Other pockets of logic:

1. **Countries and cities are feminine** — مِصْر (Miṣr, Egypt) is feminine; القاهرة مدينة جميلة (al-Qāhira madīna jamīla, "Cairo is a beautiful city") — and مدينة itself is feminine by its ة.
2. **Natural forces and elements** lean feminine in the classical core vocabulary: شَمْس (sun), أَرْض (earth), نَار (fire), رِيح (wind), حَرْب (war) — all feminine without any ة.
3. **Letters of the alphabet and the names of Quranic chapters** are treated as feminine by convention.
4. **Collectives and many animals**: نَحْل (naḥl, bees) feminine.

And then, the honest remainder: a large territory where there is no logic at all, only history. بَاب (bāb, door) is masculine; نَافِذَة (nāfidha, window) is feminine by ة; كُرْسِيّ (kursiyy, chair) is masculine; طَاوِلَة (ṭāwila, table) feminine. For these, gender is simply part of the word's identity, memorized with it.

Strategy: exploit the pockets (paired body parts → feminine is a genuinely good bet), mark every new noun with m./f. in your notes, and let frequency do what logic can't.
I wrote الرجال كبار for 'the men are tall/big' and my teacher said it was right, but السيارات كبار was wrong. Both are plurals! What's the difference?

Your teacher just handed you the cleanest demonstration of the human/non-human split in Arabic agreement.

**الرِّجَالُ كِبَارٌ** (ar-rijālu kibārun) — "The men are big/grown." ✓
**السَّيَّارَاتُ كَبِيرَةٌ** (as-sayyārātu kabīratun) — "The cars are big." ✓ — with كِبَار corrected to كَبِيرَة.

The difference is not the plural; it's **what kind of plural**. Arabic agreement sorts plurals into two species:

**Human (rational) plurals** keep full plural agreement — masculine plural كِبَار for men, feminine plural for women:

- **الْمُعَلِّمُونَ مُخْلِصُونَ** (al-muʿallimūna mukhliṣūna) — the (male) teachers are devoted
- **الْمُعَلِّمَاتُ مُخْلِصَاتٌ** (al-muʿallimātu mukhliṣātun) — the (female) teachers are devoted
- **الأَطْفَالُ صِغَارٌ** (al-aṭfālu ṣighārun) — the children are small (صغار, plural of صغير — broken plural adjective for humans)

**Non-human plurals** collapse to feminine singular, no matter the gender of the singular or the shape of the plural:

- **الْكِلَابُ كَبِيرَةٌ** (al-kilābu kabīratun) — the dogs are big (dogs: animals, things-rule)
- **الْأَشْجَارُ عَالِيَةٌ** (al-ashjāru ʿāliyatun) — the trees are tall
- **هَذِهِ الْمُدُنُ قَدِيمَةٌ** (hādhihi l-mudunu qadīmatun) — these cities are old

Why does Arabic do this? The traditional explanation is conceptual: a group of *things* is perceived as one collective mass — a single unit that grammar dresses in the default collective costume, feminine singular. A group of *people* remains a society of individuals, each counted by the agreement. Whether or not the story is historical truth, it predicts behavior perfectly.

Your two sentences are the perfect minimal pair to memorize: **men → plural agreement (كبار), cars → feminine singular (كبيرة)**. One question classifies every plural you'll ever meet: *could it talk back?* If yes, plural agreement. If no, feminine singular.
سؤال سريع: هل الشمس مذكر أم مؤنث؟ والقمر؟

**الشمس مؤنثة، والقمر مذكر.**
(Ash-shams mu'annatha, wa-l-qamar mudhakkar.)

- **الشَّمْسُ سَاخِنَةٌ** (ash-shamsu sākhinatun — The sun is hot): الصفة «ساخنة» مؤنثة لأن الشمس مؤنثة.
- **الْقَمَرُ مُنِيرٌ** (al-qamaru munīrun — The moon is bright): الصفة «منير» مذكرة لأن القمر مذكر.

وهذه صدفة جميلة تساعدك على الحفظ: كلمة **شمس** تبدأ بحرف **شمسي**، وكلمة **قمر** تبدأ بحرف **قمري**. فالشمس مثال الحروف الشمسية، والقمر مثال الحروف القمرية، في النحو وفي النطق معًا.
(Wa-hādhihi ṣudfa jamīla: kalima **shams** tabda'u bi-ḥarf shamsī, wa-kalima **qamar** bi-ḥarf qamarī.)

قاعدة عامة: جنس الكلمة في العربية — مذكر أو مؤنث — صفة من صفات الكلمة نفسها، يُحفظ معها كما يُحفظ معناها. لا توجد قاعدة من المعنى؛ فالشمس ليست «أنثى»، لكن كلمتها مؤنثة.
(Qāʿida ʿāmma: jins al-kalima ṣifa min ṣifāt al-kalima nafsihā, yuḥfaẓu maʿahā kamā yuḥfaẓu maʿnāhā.)

اختبر نفسك: **البحر** (al-baḥr — the sea) مذكر: البحر واسع. و**الصحراء** (aṣ-ṣaḥrā' — the desert) مؤنثة: الصحراء واسعة.
(Ikhtabir nafsak: al-baḥr mudhakkar — al-baḥru wāsiʿ. Wa-ṣ-ṣaḥrā' mu'annatha — aṣ-ṣaḥrā'u wāsiʿa.)
What's the proper reply to السلام عليكم? I've heard a very long version and short ones.

The greeting is **السَّلَامُ عَلَيْكُمْ** (as-salāmu ʿalaykum) — "Peace be upon you." (It is a religious greeting in origin — a prayer for the other person's safety — and today it is also simply the default formal hello across the Arabic-speaking world, used by people of all backgrounds in formal settings.)

The reply mirrors it and adds one word:

**وَعَلَيْكُمُ السَّلَامُ**
wa-ʿalaykumu s-salām
"And upon you be peace."

The full, most formal reply extends it:

**وَعَلَيْكُمُ السَّلَامُ وَرَحْمَةُ اللهِ وَبَرَكَاتُهُ**
wa-ʿalaykumu s-salāmu wa-raḥmatu llāhi wa-barakātuh
"And upon you be peace, and God's mercy, and His blessings."

How the levels work in real life:

- **The mirror reply** (وعليكم السلام) is always sufficient and always correct.
- **The full reply** is common in religious settings, formal occasions, and much of the Gulf; using it is never wrong, just warmer.
- **Shorter in practice**: you'll hear سلام (salām) as a casual standalone hello, and the reply can be a warm وعليكم السلام with a smile — or **أهلًا** (ahlan) in relaxed company.
- **Who starts**: the greeting is offered first by the one arriving, the younger to the older, the rider to the walker in the classical etiquette — in modern offices, simply whoever speaks first.

Two learner notes. First, pronunciation: ʿalaykum begins with the deep ع — 'alaykum with a plain glottal stop is understood everywhere, but the ع is worth practicing since you'll say this phrase daily. Second, non-Muslims both receive and return this greeting across the Arab world — returning it is ordinary politeness, and Arabs do not expect visitors to add the religious extension unless they wish to.
صباح الخير means 'good morning', but the reply I hear isn't the same words back. What do people actually say?

Arabic morning greetings work as call and response — the reply is a *different*, matching phrase:

**صَبَاحُ الْخَيْرِ** (ṣabāḥu l-khayr) — "Morning of goodness" → reply: **صَبَاحُ النُّورِ** (ṣabāḥu n-nūr) — "Morning of light."

The evening pair mirrors it:

**مَسَاءُ الْخَيْرِ** (masā'u l-khayr) — "Evening of goodness" → reply: **مَسَاءُ النُّورِ** (masā'u n-nūr) — "Evening of light."

Both are iḍāfa constructions — "morning-of goodness," "morning-of light" — so you're practicing grammar every time you say hello. Note the sun-letter assimilations inside them: an-nūr (ن is a sun letter) — never "al-nūr" in careful speech.

Around the pair, real life adds options:

- **صَبَاحُ الْوَرْدِ** (ṣabāḥu l-ward, "morning of roses") and **صَبَاحُ الْفُلِّ** (ṣabāḥu l-full, "morning of jasmine") — warmer, poetic replies you'll hear in Egypt and the Levant, especially to people one likes.
- In the **Gulf**, صباح الخير is answered the same way, and you'll also hear **هلا** (halā) as an all-purpose warm hello.
- **أهلًا** (ahlan) works at any hour as a neutral "welcome/hello" reply when you blank on the pair.

Timing etiquette: صباح الخير is safe until noon-ish; after that مساء الخير takes over, though the boundary is social, not legal — a صباح الخير at 12:30 draws smiles, not corrections. And when *you* are greeted first, the nūr reply is the graceful move: it returns the wish upgraded, light for goodness, which is the whole spirit of Arabic greeting exchanges — each side tries to out-warm the other.
People around me say إن شاء الله، ما شاء الله, and الحمد لله constantly, in situations I can't predict. What is each one actually doing?

These three phrases are social instruments as much as religious expressions — each does a specific job in conversation. Descriptively, here is what you're hearing:

**إِنْ شَاءَ الله** (in shā' Allāh) — literally "if God willed/wills."
Its job: it attaches to **anything future**. "I'll finish it tomorrow, in shā' Allāh" marks the plan as sincere but humble — the future is not fully ours to promise. In practice it ranges from devout hope to polite softness: it can be a firm "yes, God willing," a hopeful "let's see," or occasionally a gentle maybe. Tone, relationship, and what happens next tell you which. Learners should use it for their own future plans — it is the natural way to make an appointment in much of the Arab world — and hear it without assuming evasion.

**مَا شَاءَ الله** (mā shā' Allāh) — literally "what God willed (has come to be)."
Its job: **admiration with protection**. Said at a beautiful child, a new car, a success, good news: it admires while explicitly crediting God, which in the culture's etiquette guards the admired thing against envy. If someone shows you their baby or their new shop and you say only "beautiful!", a kind host may prompt the phrase. Using it when you compliment is deeply appreciated.

**الْحَمْدُ لِله** (al-ḥamdu lillāh) — "Praise/thanks belongs to God."
Its job: **gratitude and contentment**, in both directions of fortune. It is the standard answer to "how are you?" (I'm well — al-ḥamdu lillāh), the response to good news, the word after eating, after sneezing, after recovering — and also, strikingly, after *bad* news, where it means acceptance: things are as they are, and gratitude persists. Context sets the temperature.

A learner's rule of thumb: **in shā' Allāh faces forward, mā shā' Allāh faces someone else's good fortune, al-ḥamdu lillāh faces your own situation.** Use them respectfully and descriptively as your hosts do; nobody will mistake a sincere attempt, and the phrases will open more warmth than any other ten words you can learn.
How do I address people politely in Arabic — teachers, elders, officials? I don't want to just use names.

Arabic has a rich address system, and using it well earns instant goodwill. The workhorses:

**أُسْتَاذ** (ustādh) — "professor/teacher," but in daily life a general respectful address for an educated man or any man you want to honor: يا أستاذ (yā ustādh, "sir/professor…"). Its feminine is **أُسْتَاذَة** (ustādha). In Egypt, ustādh is the default polite way to get a stranger's attention — the equivalent of "excuse me, sir."

**حَضْرَتُك** (ḥaḍratuk) — literally "your presence," the formal "you" of respect in Egyptian and media Arabic: **حضرتك** from **حَضْرَتُكَ** (ḥaḍratuka, to a man) / **حَضْرَتُكِ** (ḥaḍratuki, to a woman). You use it instead of أنت when addressing officials, elders, and customers you serve: تفضل يا فندم؟ Egyptian service speech layers **يا فندم** (yā fandam, from Turkish efendim) on top — "at your service, sir/madam."

More of the shelf:

- **دُكْتُور** (duktūr) — for doctors and PhDs, and in Egypt generously for university teachers generally.
- **يَا حَاجّ** (yā ḥājj) / **يَا حَاجَّة** (yā ḥājja) — respectful address for an older man/woman (originally one who has made the pilgrimage; used socially for elders whether or not they have — stated descriptively, it's an honorific of age).
- **سَيِّدِي** (sayyidī) — "my lord/sir," formal and somewhat old-fashioned or military; **سَيِّدَتِي** (sayyidatī) "madam."
- **يَا شَيْخ** (yā shaykh) — for a religious scholar, and in the Gulf a title of rulers and elders.
- Professional titles stick to names: **المهندس أحمد** (al-muhandis Aḥmad, "Engineer Ahmad"), **الدكتور سامي** — title-first-name is the warm professional norm.

Two rules of thumb. When in doubt with an older person or an official, **ustādh/ḥaḍratuk** territory is always safe. And address is asymmetric by design: you may be answered with your bare name or ابنِي (ibnī, "my son") by an elder — that is affection flowing down the same system, not disrespect flowing up.
Give me the polite essentials: 'please' and 'thank you' — but I hear several versions of each.

Because Arabic politeness runs on registers, you get a small shelf of each. Learn one default of each, then the variants as they come.

**Please:**

- **مِنْ فَضْلِكَ** (min faḍlik) — the universal default. Literally "from your kindness." To a man: min faḍli**ka**; to a woman: min faḍli**ki** — in speech both sound like "min faḍlak / min faḍlik" and Egyptians say **من فضلك** for everyone without fuss.
- **لَوْ سَمَحْتَ** (law samaḥt) — "if you'd permit" — the everyday Egyptian/Levantine "excuse me, please" for getting attention and making requests. لو سمحتِ (law samaḥti) to a woman.
- **بَعْدَ إِذْنِكَ** (baʿda idhnik) — "with your permission," softer and more formal, common in the Gulf and Levant.

**Thank you:**

- **شُكْرًا** (shukran) — the default everywhere. Upgrade: **شُكْرًا جَزِيلًا** (shukran jazīlan, "thank you very much"), **أَلْف شُكْر** (alf shukr, "a thousand thanks," Egyptian warmth).
- Replies to thanks: **عَفْوًا** (ʿafwan, "you're welcome" — literally "pardon"), **عَلَى الرَّحْبِ وَالسَّعَةِ** (ʿalā r-raḥbi wa-s-saʿa, formal "with open arms"), and the beloved Levantine/Egyptian **الله يُسَلِّمُك** (Allāhu yusallimuk — "may God keep you safe"), said by the thanked person as a blessing back.
- For a service or a meal, Egyptians thank with **تِسْلَم إِيْدَك** (tislam īdak, "may your hand be safe/blessed") — to the cook, the maker, anyone whose hands did the work.

One caution and one encouragement. The caution: **shukran alone is never rude**, but Arabs notice and love the upgrades — alf shukr and tislam īdak land like gifts. The encouragement: Arabic thanking is often a *volley* — thanks, blessing back, counter-blessing — and joining the volley, even clumsily, is the fastest social win available to a learner.
How do I say goodbye properly in Arabic? I know مع السلامة but I don't know what to answer when someone says it to me.

**مَعَ السَّلَامَةِ** (maʿa s-salāma) — "with safety" — is the standard warm goodbye: go with safety. And it has a set reply, which is what you're missing:

**الله يُسَلِّمُك** (Allāhu yusallimuk) — "may God keep you safe." This is the expected answer to maʿa s-salāma across Egypt and the Levant. The exchange is a matched pair, like the morning greetings: safety wished, safety blessed back.

The rest of the goodbye shelf:

- **إِلَى اللِّقَاءِ** (ilā l-liqā') — "until the meeting" — the neutral, slightly formal goodbye, safe everywhere, the one textbooks teach.
- **أَرَاكَ غَدًا** (arāka ghadan) — "see you tomorrow" (أراكِ arāki to a woman) — أراك لاحقًا (arāka lāḥiqan, "see you later") for vaguer plans.
- **تُصْبِحُ عَلَى خَيْرٍ** (tuṣbiḥu ʿalā khayr) — "may you wake to goodness" — good night. Its set reply is a small poem: **وَأَنْتَ مِنْ أَهْلِهِ** (wa-anta min ahlihi) — "and you are among its people" (i.e., among the people of goodness). To a woman: تُصْبِحِينَ عَلَى خَيْر (tuṣbiḥīna ʿalā khayr), reply وَأَنْتِ مِنْ أَهْلِهَا (wa-anti min ahlihā).
- **فِي أَمَانِ الله** (fī amāni llāh) — "in God's protection" — a tender, older-register farewell.
- Casual and modern: **بَاي** (bāy, borrowed "bye") among young people, and **سَلَام** (salām) as a breezy sign-off.

Notice the pattern across this whole family of lessons: Arabic leave-taking, like its greeting, is built from **matched pairs** — a wish and a blessing that answers it. Learn the pairs as units (maʿa s-salāma → Allāh yusallimak; tuṣbiḥ ʿalā khayr → wa-anta min ahlihi) and you will always have the next line, which is most of what sounding polite actually is.
كيف أسأل شخصًا عن حاله بالعربية؟ سمعت «كيف حالك» و«إزيك» و«كيفك»، فما الفرق؟

كلها تعني «كيف حالك؟»، والفرق بينها هو الفرق بين الفصحى والعاميات.
(Kulluhā taʿnī "kayfa ḥāluk?", wa-l-farq baynahā huwa l-farq bayna l-fuṣḥā wa-l-ʿāmmiyyāt.)

**في الفصحى:** **كَيْفَ حَالُكَ؟** (kayfa ḥāluka — to a man)، **كَيْفَ حَالُكِ؟** (kayfa ḥāluki — to a woman). هذه هي الصيغة الرسمية، وتُستعمل في الكتابة والمناسبات الرسمية وفي كل بلد عربي.
(Fī l-fuṣḥā: kayfa ḥāluka / kayfa ḥāluki.)

**في مصر:** **إِزَّيَّك؟** (izzayyak — to a man)، **إِزَّيِّك؟** (izzayyik — to a woman). كلمة مصرية مشهورة أصلها «إزاي» أي «كيف» بلغة مصر.
(Fī Miṣr: izzayyak / izzayyik.)

**في الشام:** **كِيفَك؟** (kīfak — to a man)، **كِيفِك؟** (kīfik — to a woman). وفي الخليج ستسمع **شلونك؟** (shlōnak — "how is your color/state").
(Fī sh-Shām: kīfak / kīfik. Wa-fī l-Khalīj: shlōnak.)

والإجابات: **بِخَيْر، الْحَمْدُ لِله** (bi-khayr, al-ḥamdu lillāh — well, praise God)، أو **تمام** (tamām — great/all good)، أو **كويس** (kuwayyis — good، مصرية).
(Wa-l-ijābāt: bi-khayr, al-ḥamdu lillāh; tamām; kuwayyis.)

ثم اسأل أنت: **وَأَنْتَ؟** (wa-anta? — and you؟) أو **وَأَنْتَ كَيْفَ حَالُكَ؟**
(Thumma is'al anta: wa-anta?)

نصيحتي: تعلّم صيغة واحدة فصيحة (كيف حالك) وصيغة بلد ستزوره. الأولى تُفهم في كل مكان، والثانية تفتح القلوب.
(Naṣīḥatī: taʿallam ṣīgha wāḥida faṣīḥa wa-ṣīghat balad sa-tazūruhu.)
I'm visiting an Arab family for dinner. What phrases will make me a good guest?

Hospitality (الضيافة, aḍ-ḍiyāfa) is a serious art in Arab homes, and a guest has lines to deliver just as the host does. Your phrase kit:

**Arriving:**
- **أَهْلًا وَسَهْلًا** (ahlan wa-sahlan) is the *host's* line — "you've come to family and ease" — you answer it with **أَهْلًا بِكَ** (ahlan bika, to a man) / **أَهْلًا بِكِ** (ahlan biki, to a woman): "welcome to you too."
- **تَفَضَّلْ** (tafaḍḍal, to a man) / **تَفَضَّلِي** (tafaḍḍalī, to a woman) — the host's "please, come in / help yourself / after you." One word does every doorway, chair, and serving dish. Your reply can be simply **شُكْرًا** (shukran).

**At the table:**
- **الْبَيْتُ بَيْتُكَ** (al-baytu baytuk) — "the house is your house" — the host means: relax, take, ask. The graceful answer: **الله يخليك** (Allāh yikhallīk, "may God keep you" — Egyptian warmth) or شكرًا، كرمك كبير (shukran, karamuk kabīr — "thank you, your generosity is great").
- Before eating, many hosts say **بِسْمِ الله** (bismi llāh, "in God's name") — a guest who says it too, or simply waits a beat, is reading the room correctly.
- **صَحَّتَيْن** (ṣaḥḥatayn) — "two healths" — the Levantine "bon appétit," said to someone eating; reply: **عَلَى قَلْبِك** (ʿalā qalbik, "on your heart").

**Complimenting the food — the guest's main job:**
- **تِسْلَم إِيْدِك** (tislam īdik) — "blessed be your hand" — the gold-standard compliment to the cook (Egyptian/Levantine; to a man cook: tislam īdak).
- **الأَكْل لَذِيذ جِدًّا** (al-akl ladhīdh jiddan) — "the food is very delicious."

**Leaving:** expect resistance — leaving quickly is nearly rude; tea or coffee after the meal is part of the structure. On departure: **شُكْرًا عَلَى الضِّيَافَة** (shukran ʿalā ḍ-ḍiyāfa, "thank you for the hospitality") and **كَتَّر الله خَيْرَك** (kattara llāhu khayrak, "may God multiply your goodness").

One honest warning: your plate will be refilled. A firm, smiling **شَبِعْت، الحمد لله** (shabiʿt, al-ḥamdu lillāh — "I'm full, thank God") after the second refill is the culturally legible stop signal.
What do I say for congratulations in Arabic — and if I ever need it, for condolences? I want to get both registers right.

Both registers are formulaic, which is a mercy: the culture hands you exact lines, and sincerity is carried by using them, not by improvising.

**Congratulations:**

- **مَبْرُوك** (mabrūk) — the everyday word: weddings, exams, new jobs, new babies, new cars. **أَلْف مَبْرُوك** (alf mabrūk, "a thousand mabrūks") is the warmer upgrade. (Grammar note: careful MSA prefers **مُبَارَك** (mubārak, "blessed") — مبروك is the colloquial form that conquered daily life; both are understood everywhere, and مبارك is what you'll see in formal writing.)
- **عِيد مُبَارَك** (ʿīd mubārak) — "blessed Eid," the holiday greeting; the reply is **عَلَيْنَا وَعَلَيْكَ** (ʿalaynā wa-ʿalayk, "on us and on you") or simply عيد مبارك back.
- For a new baby: **يَتْرَبَّى فِي عِزِّك** (yitarabbā fī ʿizzik, Egyptian — "may he grow up in your pride/care") joins مبروك.
- For a wedding: **بِالرَّفَاءِ وَالْبَنِينَ** (bi-r-rafā'i wa-l-banīn) is the classical formula — beautiful, formal, and a bit old-fashioned; مبروك plus warm wishes is the modern default.

**Condolences** — offered descriptively, as these are phrases with religious content that Arabs use among themselves and receive graciously from anyone:

- **الْبَقَاءُ لِله** (al-baqā'u lillāh) — "eternity/permanence belongs to God" — the standard Egyptian condolence. The reply: **وَنِعْمَ بِالله** (wa-niʿma bi-llāh) or **الدَّوَامُ لِله** (ad-dawāmu lillāh, "endurance is God's").
- **عَظَّمَ اللهُ أَجْرَكَ** (ʿaẓẓama llāhu ajraka) — "may God magnify your reward (for your patience)" — widespread and formal.
- **إِنَّا لِلهِ وَإِنَّا إِلَيْهِ رَاجِعُونَ** (innā lillāhi wa-innā ilayhi rājiʿūn) — "we belong to God and to Him we return" — a Quranic phrase the bereaved themselves say on hearing of a death; as a visitor you will hear it more than you need to say it.
- The simple, always-safe human line: **أَنَا آسِف جِدًّا** (anā āsif jiddan, "I am very sorry") — آسفة (āsifa) if you are a woman.

Practical etiquette: condolences are delivered in person or by phone more than by card; a short visit, the formula, and presence matter more than eloquence. And in both registers — joy and grief — your attempt in Arabic will be received as the respect it is.
إذا قال لي شخص «صباح الخير»، فماذا أرد عليه؟

ترد عليه: **صَبَاحُ النُّورِ**.
(Taruddu ʿalayhi: ṣabāḥu n-nūr — "morning of light.")

- هو يقول: **صباح الخير** (ṣabāḥu l-khayr — morning of goodness)
- أنت ترد: **صباح النور** (ṣabāḥu n-nūr — morning of light)

هكذا تعمل التحيات العربية: السلام يُرَدّ بسلام مثله أو أجمل منه، لا بنفس الكلمات دائمًا.
(Hākadhā taʿmalu t-taḥiyyāt al-ʿarabiyya: as-salām yuraddu bi-salām mithlihi aw ajmal minhu.)

وفي المساء نفس النظام:
(Wa-fī l-masā' nafs an-niẓām:)

- **مَسَاءُ الْخَيْرِ** (masā'u l-khayr — evening of goodness)
- الرد: **مَسَاءُ النُّورِ** (masā'u n-nūr — evening of light)

وتوجد ردود أجمل في مصر والشام: **صباح الورد** (ṣabāḥu l-ward — morning of roses) و**صباح الفل** (ṣabāḥu l-full — morning of jasmine)، وهي ردود دافئة تقال للأحباب والأصدقاء.
(Wa-tūjadu rudūd ajmal: ṣabāḥu l-ward, ṣabāḥu l-full.)

وإذا نسيت كل شيء، قل **أهلًا وسهلًا** (ahlan wa-sahlan) بابتسامة؛ فهي تحية صالحة في كل وقت.
(Wa-idhā nasīta kull shay', qul ahlan wa-sahlan bi-ibtisāma.)
Teach me to ask for directions in Arabic — and more importantly, to understand the answer.

Asking is easy; the answer is the exam. Both halves, with the skeleton of a typical reply:

**Asking:**

- **أَيْنَ…؟** (ayna…?) — "Where is…?" — **أَيْنَ الْمَحَطَّةُ؟** (ayna l-maḥaṭṭa? — Where is the station?)
- **كَيْفَ أَصِلُ إِلَى…؟** (kayfa aṣilu ilā…?) — "How do I get to…?" — the most useful question shape.
- **هَلْ هُوَ قَرِيبٌ مِنْ هُنَا؟** (hal huwa qarībun min hunā?) — "Is it near here?"

**The answer's skeleton** — directions come in a fixed order: go straight, turn, landmark, side:

- **اِذْهَبْ إِلَى الْأَمَامِ** (idhhab ilā l-amām) — "Go forward/straight ahead." (اِمْشِ عَلَى طُول, imshi ʿalā ṭūl, is the Egyptian street version: "keep straight.")
- **ثُمَّ** (thumma) — "then" — the hinge word of every direction.
- **اِنْعَطِفْ يَمِينًا** (inʿaṭif yamīnan) — "turn right"; **اِنْعَطِفْ يَسَارًا** (inʿaṭif yasāran) — "turn left." (Egyptian street: خُد يمينك khud yamīnak, "take your right.")
- **عَلَى الْيَمِينِ / عَلَى الْيَسَارِ** (ʿalā l-yamīn / ʿalā l-yasār) — "on the right / on the left" (for where the thing *is*).
- **بِجَانِبِ** (bi-jānibi) — "next to"; **أَمَامَ** (amāma) — "in front of"; **خَلْفَ** (khalfa) — "behind"; **بَعْدَ** (baʿda) — "after/past"; **قَبْلَ** (qabla) — "before."
- **قَرِيبٌ / بَعِيدٌ** (qarīb / baʿīd) — near / far; **عَشْرُ دَقَائِقَ مَشْيًا** (ʿashru daqā'iqa mashyan) — "ten minutes on foot."

A full model answer, parsed: **اِمْشِ عَلَى طُول، ثُمَّ خُذْ أَوَّلَ شَارِعٍ عَلَى الْيَمِينِ؛ الْمَحَطَّةُ بَعْدَ الْبَنْكِ مُبَاشَرَةً** (imshi ʿalā ṭūl, thumma khudh awwala shāriʿin ʿalā l-yamīn; al-maḥaṭṭatu baʿda l-banki mubāsharatan) — "Go straight, then take the first street on the right; the station is right after the bank."

Survival strategy: you don't need every word — catch the landmarks (bank, mosque, bridge) and the turn words (yamīn/yasār), repeat them back with a pointing hand, and let the other person's corrections do the rest. Direction-giving in Arab cities is a contact sport; people will walk you halfway there.
I want to order coffee in Arabic — properly, including how sweet. And how do I ask for the bill?

Coffee (قهوة, qahwa) in the Arab world is a small ceremony with its own vocabulary. The MSA frame first, then the Egyptian café dialect you'll actually hear in Cairo.

**Ordering (MSA):**
- **أُرِيدُ قَهْوَةً، مِنْ فَضْلِكَ** (urīdu qahwatan, min faḍlik) — "I'd like a coffee, please."
- **قَهْوَة عَرَبِيَّة** (qahwa ʿarabiyya) — Arabic coffee (spiced, in the Gulf/Levant, served in small cups, often with dates)
- **قَهْوَة تُرْكِيَّة** (qahwa turkiyya) — Turkish-style coffee (Egypt/Levant café standard)
- **شَاي** (shāy) — tea, if coffee isn't your order; **عَصِير** (ʿaṣīr) — juice.

**The sugar scale** — this is the part natives quiz you on. For Turkish coffee in Egypt you order your sweetness by name:

- **سَادَة** (sāda) — plain, no sugar
- **عَلَى الرِّيحَة** (ʿalā r-rīḥa) — "on the scent" — a whisper of sugar (Egyptian connoisseur level)
- **مَظْبُوط** (maẓbūṭ) — "exact" — medium, the default beloved order
- **زِيَادَة** (ziyāda) — extra sweet

So the full Cairo order is one breath: **قَهْوَة مَظْبُوط، مِنْ فَضْلِك** (qahwa maẓbūṭ, min faḍlik). In dialect, "I want" becomes **عَايِز** (ʿāyiz, m.) / **عَايْزَة** (ʿāyza, f.): عايز قهوة سادة (ʿāyiz qahwa sāda).

**The bill:**
- MSA: **الْحِسَابُ، مِنْ فَضْلِكَ** (al-ḥisābu, min faḍlik) — "The bill, please."
- Egyptian street: **الحساب لو سمحت** (il-ḥisāb law samaḥt).
- To pay a taxi or small vendor: **كَمْ؟** (kam? — "How much?") is blunt but universal; politer: **بِكَمْ هَذَا؟** (bi-kam hādhā?).

One cultural note: in a traditional coffeehouse (قَهْوَة is also the word for the café itself in Egypt — "ana fī l-qahwa" means you're *at* the café), your cup may be refilled or a second ordered for you by a companion. Refusing is done warmly, with a hand on the heart and **شُكْرًا، كَفَايَة** (shukran, kifāya — "thanks, that's enough").
I tried to say 'this costs thirty pounds' and 'five books' and got corrected both times. What is Arabic doing with numbers and nouns?

You've walked into the most famously intricate corner of Arabic grammar: **number–noun agreement**, where the number's gender flips against the noun's, and the noun changes case depending on how big the number is. Take the honest tour — with the safe frames at the end.

**Numbers 3–10: gender polarity.** The number takes the *opposite* gender form from the noun:

- **خَمْسَةُ كُتُبٍ** (khamsatu kutubin) — "five books." كتاب is masculine, so "five" wears the feminine-looking form خَمْسَة. The noun is plural, genitive.
- **خَمْسُ سَيَّارَاتٍ** (khamsu sayyārātin) — "five cars." سيارة is feminine, so "five" is the bare خَمْس. Noun plural, genitive.

Yes, it feels backwards. It is backwards. Every learner says so; the system is a thousand years old and unbothered.

**Numbers 11–99: singular accusative noun.** The noun goes singular and takes -an:

- **ثَلَاثُونَ جُنَيْهًا** (thalāthūna junayhan) — "thirty pounds." (جنيه junayh is the Egyptian pound.) Your sentence: **هَذَا بِثَلَاثِينَ جُنَيْهًا** (hādhā bi-thalāthīna junayhan) — "this is (for) thirty pounds" — with ثلاثين in its -īna form after the preposition بـ.
- **عِشْرُونَ طَالِبًا** (ʿishrūna ṭāliban) — "twenty students."

**100 and 1000: singular genitive noun.**
- **مِئَةُ كِتَابٍ** (mi'atu kitābin) — "a hundred books" (literally "a hundred of book").
- **أَلْفُ سَنَةٍ** (alfu sanatin) — "a thousand years" — as in ألف ليلة وليلة, the Thousand and One Nights.

**Numbers 1–2** mostly retire: "one book" is just كِتَاب (with وَاحِد for emphasis: كتاب واحد), and "two" uses the dual: كِتَابَانِ.

**The safe frames** — what to actually say while the full system settles:
1. In speech and dialects, polarity is dropped entirely: Egyptians say **خمس كتب** (khams kutub) and **تلاتين جنيه** (talātīn ginēh) — number invariable, noun plural. Nobody will correct you in a market.
2. In MSA, if you must produce one careful pattern, master 3–10 polarity + plural noun; it covers prices, ages, and counts you'll actually say.
2. When writing a number inside a sentence, using **digits** (٣٠ جنيهًا) is common in real Arabic prose and quietly sidesteps spoken agreement — but the noun after a written 30 still takes its -an in careful style.

Your two corrections were the system working as designed, not you failing. Arabic numbers are a small mountain with a well-marked tourist path (the dialect way) and a summit route (full MSA agreement) — climb in that order.
Give me the Arabic numbers 1 to 10 as a reference — I've heard they have masculine and feminine forms.

Cardinal numbers 1–10. Arabic numbers from 3 to 10 show **gender polarity**: the form with ة pairs with masculine nouns, the bare form with feminine nouns — the opposite of what you'd expect. (Used with a masculine noun: خَمْسَةُ كُتُبٍ, "five books"; with a feminine noun: خَمْسُ سَيَّارَاتٍ, "five cars.")

| # | With masculine nouns | With feminine nouns |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | وَاحِد (wāḥid) | وَاحِدَة (wāḥida) |
| 2 | اِثْنَان (ithnān) | اِثْنَتَان (ithnatān) |
| 3 | ثَلَاثَة (thalātha) | ثَلَاث (thalāth) |
| 4 | أَرْبَعَة (arbaʿa) | أَرْبَع (arbaʿ) |
| 5 | خَمْسَة (khamsa) | خَمْس (khams) |
| 6 | سِتَّة (sitta) | سِتّ (sitt) |
| 7 | سَبْعَة (sabʿa) | سَبْع (sabʿ) |
| 8 | ثَمَانِيَة (thamāniya) | ثَمَانٍ (thamānin) |
| 9 | تِسْعَة (tisʿa) | تِسْع (tisʿ) |
| 10 | عَشَرَة (ʿashara) | عَشْر (ʿashr) |

And the architecture above ten:

| | Arabic | Transliteration |
|---|---|---|
| 11 | أَحَدَ عَشَرَ | aḥada ʿashara |
| 12 | اِثْنَا عَشَرَ | ithnā ʿashara |
| 20 | عِشْرُونَ | ʿishrūna |
| 30 | ثَلَاثُونَ | thalāthūna |
| 40 | أَرْبَعُونَ | arbaʿūna |
| 50 | خَمْسُونَ | khamsūna |
| 100 | مِئَة | mi'a |
| 200 | مِئَتَانِ | mi'atāni (dual of 100) |
| 1000 | أَلْف | alf |

Three usage notes:

1. **One and two barely work as numbers**: "one book" is كِتَابٌ وَاحِدٌ (kitābun wāḥidun) with wāḥid as an adjective after the noun; "two books" is the dual كِتَابَانِ (kitābāni). The table forms for 1–2 appear mainly in counting and in 11/12.
2. **Tens behave like masculine plurals** (-ūna/-īna endings: عِشْرُونَ / عِشْرِينَ) and combine with units as "one-and-twenty": وَاحِدٌ وَعِشْرُونَ (wāḥidun wa-ʿishrūna) — units first, then the ten, joined by وَ.
3. **In dialects, polarity is gone**: one invariable set (خمس، ست، سبع…) serves all nouns. The full polarity system is an MSA/writing skill — read it fluently first, produce it carefully second.
كيف أقول الوقت بالعربية؟ إذا كانت الساعة الثالثة والنصف مثلًا؟

بنية الوقت في العربية بسيطة: تقول **الساعة** ثم العدد الترتيبي.
(Binyat al-waqt fī l-ʿarabiyya basīṭa: taqūlu **as-sāʿa** thumma l-ʿadad at-tartībī.)

- **السَّاعَةُ الثَّالِثَةُ** (as-sāʿatu th-thālitha — three o'clock). كلمة «ساعة» مؤنثة، ولذلك العدد مؤنث: الثالثة، الرابعة، الخامسة...
(As-sāʿa kalima mu'annatha, wa-li-dhālika l-ʿadad mu'annath.)

وللدقائق كلمات خاصة:
(Wa-li-d-daqā'iq kalimāt khāṣṣa:)

- **وَالنِّصْف** (wa-n-niṣf — and a half): الساعة الثالثة والنصف = 3:30
- **وَالرُّبْع** (wa-r-rubʿ — and a quarter): الساعة الثالثة والربع = 3:15
- **إِلَّا رُبْعًا** (illā rubʿan — minus a quarter): الساعة الرابعة إلا ربعًا = 3:45، أي «الرابعة ناقص ربع»

وعبارات ستحتاجها:
(Wa-ʿibārāt sa-taḥtājuhā:)

- **كَمِ السَّاعَةُ الْآنَ؟** (kam as-sāʿatu l-ān? — What time is it now?)
- **فِي السَّاعَةِ السَّابِعَةِ** (fī s-sāʿati s-sābiʿa — at seven o'clock)
- **صَبَاحًا / مَسَاءً** (ṣabāḥan / masā'an — in the morning / in the evening): الساعة الثامنة صباحًا = 8 AM
- **ظُهْرًا** (ẓuhran — at noon)، **مُنْتَصَفُ اللَّيْلِ** (muntaṣafu l-layl — midnight)

وفي العامية المصرية ستسمع: **الساعة تلاتة ونص** (is-sāʿa talāta wi-nuṣṣ — 3:30) — بلا «الساعة» المؤنثة الرسمية، وبالأعداد العادية.
(Wa-fī l-ʿāmmiyya al-miṣriyya: is-sāʿa talāta wi-nuṣṣ.)

ملاحظة: عندما تقول «عندي موعد الساعة الخامسة»، فأنت تستعمل نفس البنية تمامًا.
(Mulāḥaẓa: nafs al-binya taʿmalu li-l-mawāʿīd — appointments.)
Teach me the days of the week in Arabic — and is the weekend really Friday-Saturday?

The days, with their hidden numbers:

| Day | Arabic | Transliteration | Root logic |
|---|---|---|---|
| Sunday | الْأَحَد | al-aḥad | from أَحَد — "one" (day one) |
| Monday | الِاثْنَيْن | al-ithnayn | from اِثْنَان — "two" |
| Tuesday | الثُّلَاثَاء | ath-thulāthā' | from ثَلَاثَة — "three" |
| Wednesday | الْأَرْبِعَاء | al-arbiʿā' | from أَرْبَعَة — "four" |
| Thursday | الْخَمِيس | al-khamīs | from خَمْسَة — "five" |
| Friday | الْجُمُعَة | al-jumuʿa | "the gathering" — congregational prayer day |
| Saturday | السَّبْت | as-sabt | from the Sabbath root |

Sunday through Thursday are literally numbered one to five — a fossil of the week counted from Sunday. Friday breaks the count with a name of its own, marking its religious weight (descriptively: it is the day of the midday congregational prayer, and sermons and prayer shape its rhythm).

**The weekend, honestly, by country — because it has moved:**

- **Friday–Saturday**: still the weekend in much of the region — Egypt, Jordan, Iraq, Saudi Arabia (which switched *to* Thu–Fri until 2013, then Fri–Sat), Qatar, Kuwait, and others.
- **Saturday–Sunday**: Lebanon, and the Maghreb generally (Morocco, Tunisia, Algeria), aligning with Europe.
- **The UAE** moved in January 2022 to **Saturday–Sunday**, with Friday as a half working day in the public sector — the region's most-watched experiment in aligning with global markets.

So "the weekend is Friday–Saturday" is a good default for the Gulf and Egypt, but check the country before you schedule. One constant: **Friday midday** is prayer time everywhere — offices, shops, and officials pause regardless of which days form the weekend.

Useful frames: **يَوْمُ الْجُمُعَةِ** (yawmu l-jumuʿa, "on Friday"), **غَدًا** (ghadan, tomorrow), **أَمْسِ** (amsi, yesterday), **الْأُسْبُوعُ الْقَادِمُ** (al-usbūʿu l-qādim, next week).
If I get sick or hurt while traveling in an Arabic-speaking country, what exact phrases do I need?

These are worth memorizing cold. Medical and emergency Arabic, MSA forms that work everywhere:

**Getting help:**
- **سَاعِدُونِي!** (sāʿidūnī!) — "Help me!" (to a group; to one man: سَاعِدْنِي sāʿidnī)
- **اِتَّصِلُوا بِالْإِسْعَافِ!** (ittaṣilū bi-l-isʿāf!) — "Call an ambulance!"
- **أَحْتَاجُ طَبِيبًا** (aḥtāju ṭabīban) — "I need a doctor."
- **أَيْنَ أَقْرَبُ مُسْتَشْفَى؟** (ayna aqrabu mustashfan?) — "Where is the nearest hospital?" (مُسْتَشْفَى mustashfā is one of Arabic's famous look-alike words — a Form X place noun: "place where cure is sought.")

**Describing the problem:**
- **عِنْدِي أَلَمٌ هُنَا** (ʿindī alamun hunā) — "I have a pain here." (Point. This phrase plus pointing has carried more travelers than any other.)
- **أَشْعُرُ بِـ…** (ashʿuru bi-…) — "I feel…" + **دُوَار** (duwār, dizziness), **غَثَيَان** (ghathayān, nausea), **حُمَّى** (ḥummā, fever)
- **عِنْدِي حَسَاسِيَّةٌ مِنْ…** (ʿindī ḥasāsiyyatun min…) — "I am allergic to…" — learn this one with *your* allergen filled in before you travel.
- **أَتَنَاوَلُ هَذَا الدَّوَاءَ** (atanāwalu hādhā d-dawā') — "I take this medicine" (show the bottle).
- **كَسْرٌ / جُرْحٌ / نَزِيفٌ** (kasr / jurḥ / nazīf) — a fracture / a wound / bleeding.

**At the pharmacy** (صَيْدَلِيَّة ṣaydaliyya — pharmacies are excellent and pharmacists are front-line medicine in much of the Arab world):
- **هَلْ عِنْدَكَ دَوَاءٌ لِلصُّدَاعِ؟** (hal ʿindaka dawā'un li-ṣ-ṣudāʿ?) — "Do you have medicine for a headache?"

A calm note: English is widely spoken in hospitals in the Gulf, Jordan, and Lebanon, and French in the Maghreb — but these phrases work in every clinic, village, and taxi in between, and opening in Arabic changes how hard people work to help you. The one to drill until it's reflexive: **عندي ألم هنا**. Everything else can be pointed at in a phrasebook.
أريد أن أشتري شيئًا في سوق عربي. ما العبارات التي أحتاجها؟

هذه عبارات السوق الأساسية، بالفصحى مع لمسات عامية حيث تنفع.
(Hādhihi ʿibārāt as-sūq al-asāsiyya.)

**السؤال عن السعر:**
(Is-su'āl ʿan as-siʿr:)

- **بِكَمْ هَذَا؟** (bi-kam hādhā? — How much is this?)
- **بِكَمْ هَذِهِ؟** (bi-kam hādhihi? — How much is this? — feminine)
- **كَمْ ثَمَنُهُ؟** (kam thamanuhu? — What is its price?)

**ردودك على السعر:**
(Rudūduk ʿalā s-siʿr:)

- **غَالٍ جِدًّا!** (ghālin jiddan! — Too expensive!)
- **هَلْ يُمْكِنُ أَنْ تُخَفِّضَ السِّعْرَ؟** (hal yumkinu an tukhaffiḍa s-siʿr? — Can you lower the price?)
- **هَلْ هَذَا آخِرُ سِعْرٍ؟** (hal hādhā ākhiru siʿr? — Is this your last price?)
- **سَآخُذُهُ** (sa-ākhudhuhu — I'll take it) / **لَا، شُكْرًا** (lā, shukran — no, thank you)

وفي مصر ستسمع وتقول: **بكام ده؟** (bi-kām da? — How much is this?)، ويرد البائع: **آخر كلام خمسين** (ākhir kalām khamsīn — "fifty, final word").
(Wa-fī Miṣr: bi-kām da? Wa-yaruddu l-bā'iʿ: ākhir kalām khamsīn.)

قاعدة اجتماعية: المساومة متوقعة في الأسواق التقليدية والمحلات الصغيرة، لكنها غير مناسبة في المحلات ذات الأسعار الثابتة والمولات. ابدأ دائمًا بابتسامة، ولا تساوم على شيء لا تنوي شراءه؛ فالمساومة عند العرب حديث اجتماعي بقدر ما هي تجارة.
(Qāʿida ijtimāʿiyya: al-musāwama mutawaqqaʿa fī l-aswāq at-taqlīdiyya, lākinnahā ghayr munāsiba fī l-maḥallāt dhāt al-asʿār ath-thābita.)

وإذا نجحت الصفقة، يقول البائع لك: **مَبْرُوك عَلَيْكَ** (mabrūk ʿalayk — congratulations to you)، وترد: **الله يُبَارِكُ فِيكَ** (Allāhu yubāriku fīk — may God bless you).
(Wa-idhā najaḥati ṣ-ṣafqa, yaqūlu l-bā'iʿ: mabrūk ʿalayk, wa-taruddu: Allāhu yubāriku fīk.)
Give me transport Arabic: taxis, tickets, stations — the phrases that get me around.

The getting-around kit, MSA with the street forms flagged:

**Places and vehicles:**
- **مَحَطَّة** (maḥaṭṭa) — station; **مَحَطَّةُ الْقِطَارِ** (maḥaṭṭatu l-qiṭār) — train station
- **قِطَار** (qiṭār) — train; **حَافِلَة** (ḥāfila) — bus (Egyptian: أُوتُوبِيس utūbīs); **سَيَّارَةُ أُجْرَةٍ** (sayyāratu ujra) — taxi (Egyptian: تاكسي taksi, ميكروباص mīkrūbāṣ for the shared minivans)
- **تَذْكِرَة** (tadhkira) — ticket; **تَذْكِرَةُ ذَهَابٍ وَعَوْدَةٍ** (tadhkiratu dhahābin wa-ʿawda) — round-trip ticket (literally "going and returning")
- **مَطَار** (maṭār) — airport

**In the taxi:**
- **أُرِيدُ أَنْ أَذْهَبَ إِلَى…** (urīdu an adhhaba ilā…) — "I want to go to…" (Egyptian: **عَايِز أَرُوح…** ʿāyiz arūḥ…)
- **شَغِّلِ الْعَدَّادَ، مِنْ فَضْلِكَ** (shaghghili l-ʿaddāda, min faḍlik) — "Turn on the meter, please." (In Egypt this sentence marks you as no fool.)
- **اِنْزِلْ هُنَا، مِنْ فَضْلِكَ** (inzil hunā, min faḍlik) — "Stop here, please" (literally "let me down here").
- **عَلَى مَهْلِكَ** (ʿalā mahlik) — "take your time / slow down, no rush."

**On the train/bus:**
- **هَلْ هَذَا الْمَقْعَدُ فَارِغٌ؟** (hal hādhā l-maqʿadu fārighun?) — "Is this seat free?"
- **هَلْ يَقِفُ هَذَا الْقِطَارُ فِي…؟** (hal yaqifu hādhā l-qiṭāru fī…?) — "Does this train stop in…?"
- **مَتَى نَصِلُ؟** (matā naṣilu?) — "When do we arrive?"

**Understanding the answer:** **مُبَاشَر** (mubāshar) — direct/nonstop; **تَغْيِير فِي** (taghyīr fī…) — "change at…"; **الرَّصِيفُ الثَّانِي** (ar-raṣīfu th-thānī) — platform two.

Dialect realism: transport is where dialect runs the show — drivers will answer in pure ʿāmmiyya. But MSA questions are understood by every driver in the Arab world, and a written destination (show the address on your phone) closes any gap your accent opens. The taxi trio to drill: destination + شغل العداد + انزل هنا.
كيف أطلب القهوة في مقهى عربي؟ أريد العبارات كاملة من الدخول حتى الحساب.

بكل سرور — هذه زيارة كاملة إلى المقهى بالعبارات:
(Bi-kull surūr — hādhihi ziyāra kāmila ilā l-maqhā bi-l-ʿibārāt:)

**١- الدخول والجلوس:** يقول النادل: **تَفَضَّلْ** (tafaḍḍal — please, come in/sit). وتقول أنت: **طَاوِلَة لِشَخْصَيْنِ، مِنْ فَضْلِكَ** (ṭāwila li-shakhṣayn, min faḍlik — a table for two, please).
(Ad-dukhūl wa-l-julūs.)

**٢- الطلب:** **أُرِيدُ قَهْوَةً، مِنْ فَضْلِكَ** (urīdu qahwatan, min faḍlik — I would like a coffee, please). وحدد السكر: **سَادَة** (sāda — no sugar)، **مَظْبُوط** (maẓbūṭ — medium)، **زِيَادَة** (ziyāda — extra sweet). وفي مصر: **عايز قهوة مظبوط** (ʿāyiz qahwa maẓbūṭ).
(Aṭ-ṭalab. Wa-ḥaddid as-sukkar.)

**٣- إضافات:** **وَكُوبَ مَاءٍ أَيْضًا** (wa-kūba mā'in ayḍan — and a glass of water too)، **هَلْ عِنْدَكُمْ عَصِيرٌ طَازَجٌ؟** (hal ʿindakum ʿaṣīrun ṭāzaj? — do you have fresh juice?).
(Iḍāfāt.)

**٤- الحساب:** **الْحِسَابُ، مِنْ فَضْلِكَ** (al-ḥisābu, min faḍlik — the bill, please). وفي مصر: **الحساب لو سمحت** (il-ḥisāb law samaḥt).
(Al-ḥisāb.)

**٥- الشكر والمغادرة:** **شُكْرًا جَزِيلًا** (shukran jazīlan — thank you very much)، وتغادر بـ**مَعَ السَّلَامَةِ** (maʿa s-salāma).
(Ash-shukr wa-l-mughādara.)

ملاحظة ثقافية: كلمة **قهوة** نفسها تعني المشروب والمقهى في مصر؛ فإذا قال صديقك «أنا في القهوة» فهو جالس في المقهى لا في الكوب.
(Mulāḥaẓa thaqāfiyya: kalima **qahwa** nafsuhā taʿnī l-mashrūb wa-l-maqhā fī Miṣr.)
Be straight with me: is Modern Standard Arabic actually anyone's language? What do people speak at home?

Straight answer: **MSA is nobody's mother tongue.** No child anywhere grows up speaking Modern Standard Arabic at the kitchen table. Every Arab child learns a **dialect** (عامية, ʿāmmiyya) at home — Egyptian, Levantine, Gulf, Maghrebi, and dozens of sub-varieties — and then learns MSA at school, the way you'd learn a formal, written, pan-Arab register of your own language.

The technical term is **diglossia**: two forms of one language living side by side, each with its territory:

- **Dialect's territory**: home, street, friends, humor, songs, TV comedy and drama dialogue, texting, the market, the taxi — nearly all spoken life.
- **MSA's territory** (الفصحى, al-fuṣḥā — "the eloquent/pure one"): news broadcasts, newspapers and books, formal speeches, official documents, religious sermons, exams, and any writing meant to last or to travel across countries.

What this means practically:

1. **MSA is understood everywhere** — an Egyptian and a Moroccan who can't follow each other's dialects switch toward MSA and meet in the middle. It is the Arab world's shared formal floor.
2. **Nobody chats in pure MSA.** Speaking textbook MSA in a café sounds the way speaking legal-contract English would in a diner: comprehensible, correct, and unmistakably foreign. Arabs find it charming from learners, not ridiculous — but they will answer you in dialect.
3. **The dialects are not "broken MSA."** They are full systems with their own grammars, some features older than MSA's standardization, some newer. Linguists describe them as sister varieties, not corruptions.
4. **Classical Arabic** — the language of the Quran and classical literature — is MSA's ancestor and close relative; MSA is its modernized, streamlined descendant. A reader of MSA can approach classical texts with effort; the reverse journey is harder.

So the learning strategy writes itself: MSA gives you reading, writing, formal speech, and a passport understood in 20+ countries. A dialect gives you *people* — in one region. You need the first for literacy and the second for life, in that order, and anyone who tells you one makes the other unnecessary is selling something.
Show me the same everyday sentence in MSA, Egyptian, and Levantine so I can feel the dialect differences.

The sentence: **"I want to go now."** Three Arabics, side by side:

**MSA (الفصحى):**
**أُرِيدُ أَنْ أَذْهَبَ الْآنَ**
urīdu an adhhaba l-ān
The full machinery: urīdu "I want" + an + subjunctive adhhaba "go" + al-ān "now." Every word is dictionary Arabic.

**Egyptian (مصري):**
**عَايِز أَرُوح دِلْوَقْتِي**
ʿāyiz arūḥ dilwa'ti
Three changes at once: "want" is a different word entirely — **عايز** (ʿāyiz, from a root meaning "to need/lack"); "go" is **أروح** (arūḥ, from راح rāḥ, a verb MSA keeps for "to go" only in poetry and set phrases); "now" is **دلوقتي** (dilwa'ti, literally "this time"). Not one content word survives from the MSA version — and an Egyptian says this fifty times a day.

**Levantine (شامي):**
**بَدِّي رُوح هَلَّق**
biddī rūḥ halla'
"Want" is **بدي** (biddī — "my desire," from وِدّ widd); "go" again uses rūḥ but without the a- prefix (Levantine drops it); "now" is **هلّق** (halla'). Shorter, lighter, unmistakably Beirut/Damascus.

A second round, **"What do you want?"** to a man:
- MSA: **مَاذَا تُرِيدُ؟** (mādhā turīdu?)
- Egyptian: **عَايِز إِيه؟** (ʿāyiz ēh?)
- Levantine: **شُو بَدَّك؟** (shū biddak?) — شو (shū, "what") is the Levantine signature word.

Patterns to notice across both rounds: dialects **shorten** (prefixes and endings drop), **swap core vocabulary** (want/now/what are different words, not just different pronunciations), and **share more with each other than the extremes suggest** — Egyptian and Levantine both chose rūḥ for "go." The dialects form a family with strong resemblances and real borders; MSA sits above them all as the written roof.
Which everyday words change completely between MSA and the dialects? I want the ones that will actually trip me.

The high-frequency traitors — words where the dialect doesn't just pronounce MSA differently but uses a different word altogether:

**Car**
- MSA: **سَيَّارَة** (sayyāra)
- Egypt: **عَرَبِيَّة** (ʿarabiyya) — literally "Arabian (fem.)"! The word that means "Arabic (language)" in MSA means "car" in Cairo. Context — and the wheels — disambiguate.

**Bread**
- MSA: **خُبْز** (khubz)
- Egypt: **عَيْش** (ʿaysh) — which in MSA means "life/living." In Egypt, bread *is* life, and the word says so. (Levant keeps khubz.)

**Now**
- MSA: **الْآن** (al-ān)
- Egypt: **دِلْوَقْتِي** (dilwa'ti); Levant: **هَلَّق** (halla'); Gulf: **الْحِين** (al-ḥīn)

**Money**
- MSA: **مَال** (māl, wealth) / **نُقُود** (nuqūd, cash)
- Nearly all dialects: **فُلُوس** (fulūs) — originally the plural of فلس (fals, a small copper coin). "With money" = معايا فلوس in Egypt.

**Very**
- MSA: **جِدًّا** (jiddan)
- Egypt: **أَوِي** (awi); Levant: **كْتِير** (ktīr, from "much"); Gulf: **وَايِد** (wāyid)

**Good/fine**
- MSA: **جَيِّد** (jayyid)
- Egypt: **كُوَيِّس** (kuwayyis); Levant: **مْنِيح** (mnīḥ)

**To see**
- MSA: **رَأَى** (ra'ā)
- Egypt/Levant: **شَاف** (shāf) — يشوف (yishūf). "Did you see?" is شفت؟ (shuft?) from Casablanca to Baghdad, whatever the textbook says.

**To speak**
- MSA: **تَكَلَّمَ** (takallama)
- Egypt: **اِتْكَلِّم** (itkallim) keeps the root; Levant often **حَكَى** (ḥakā, "to talk/chat") — while MSA حكى means "to narrate/imitate."

The meta-lesson: the words that change most are the *smallest, commonest* ones — now, very, money, see, car, bread. Grammar words and daily-life nouns are where dialects live their own lives; formal vocabulary (politics, science, religion, news) stays close to MSA everywhere. Learn MSA for the newspaper, and expect the street to re-teach you its fifty favorite words in your first week.
What makes Egyptian Arabic sound Egyptian? Give me its signature features.

Egyptian (مصري, maṣrī) is the most widely understood dialect — a century of Egyptian cinema and TV exported it everywhere — and it has a clear fingerprint. Five features do most of the work:

**1. ج is pronounced "g" (hard, as in "go").**
MSA جَمَل (jamal, camel) → Egyptian **جمل** pronounced **gamal**. جَدِيد (jadīd, new) → **gidīd**. This single sound announces Cairo instantly.

**2. ق collapses to a glottal stop.**
قَالَ (qāla, he said) → **قال** pronounced **'āl**. قَمَر (qamar, moon) → **'amar**. (In careful or religious words, the q survives — قرآن is always Qur'ān.)

**3. The negation wraps the verb: ma-…-sh.**
**مَا كَتَبْش** (ma katabsh) — "he didn't write." مَا + verb + ش. For nominal sentences, **مِش** (mish) does it: **أَنَا مِش طَالِب** (ana mish ṭālib) — "I'm not a student."

**4. The present tense wears a bi- prefix.**
**بِيِكْتِب** (biyiktib) — "he writes / is writing." **بَاكُل** (bākul) — "I eat." And the future takes **ha-**: **هَرُوح** (harūḥ) — "I'll go."

**5. Signature vocabulary.**
**عَايِز** (ʿāyiz, want), **إِزَّيَّك** (izzayyak, how are you), **دِلْوَقْتِي** (dilwa'ti, now), **أَوِي** (awi, very), **كَام** (kām, how much/many), **لِيه** (lēh, why), **بَرْدُه** (bardu, also/still).

Hear them combined: **أَنَا عَايِز أَرُوح دِلْوَقْتِي، مِش هَاكْتُب الْجَوَاب دَه** (ana ʿāyiz arūḥ dilwa'ti, mish haktib il-gawāb da) — "I want to go now; I'm not going to write that letter." (جواب gawāb = letter in Egyptian — in MSA it means "answer." Egypt repurposes cheerfully.)

One status note: Egyptians code-switch constantly — a Cairene professor lectures toward MSA and jokes in pure maṣrī. And because of the media legacy, speaking Egyptian *to* other Arabs works almost everywhere; they'll answer in their own dialect and you'll mostly understand each other. It is the closest thing the spoken language has to a lingua franca.
And Levantine? What makes Arabic sound like Beirut or Damascus?

Levantine (شامي, shāmī — Syrian, Lebanese, Jordanian, Palestinian) is famous for sounding soft and melodic to Arab ears, and its fingerprint is just as clear as Egypt's:

**1. بدّي (biddī) — "I want."**
From بِوِدِّي (bi-widdī, "in my desire"). **بَدِّي رُوح** (biddī rūḥ) — "I want to go." **شُو بَدَّك؟** (shū biddak?) — "What do you want?" — شو (shū, "what") is the other Levantine shibboleth; MSA's ماذا (mādhā) barely survives in casual speech.

**2. The future is رح (raḥ) or حَـ (ḥa-).**
**رَح رُوح** (raḥ rūḥ) — "I'll go." **حَ نِحْكِي بُكْرَة** (ḥa niḥkī bukra) — "we'll talk tomorrow."

**3. Present verbs drop the MSA prefix vowels and take b-.**
**بْحِبَّك** (bḥibbak) — "I love you." **بْيِحْكِي** (byiḥkī) — "he speaks/talks." Initial clusters that MSA forbids (bḥ-, kt-) are Levantine's normal music.

**4. ق → glottal stop, like Egypt — but ذ and ظ lean toward z/d sounds.**
قَلْب (qalb) → **'alb** (heart). هٰذَا (hādhā, this) → **هَاد** (hād) in many areas. Interdentals (ث ذ ظ) generally merge with stops/sibilants in city Levantine: ثَلَاثَة (thalātha, three) → **تْلَاتة** (tlāte).

**5. Signature vocabulary.**
**هَلَّق** (halla', now), **وِين** (wayn, where), **كِيفَك** (kīfak, how are you), **مْنِيح** (mnīḥ, good), **يَعْنِي** (yaʿnī — "I mean / like," the universal Levantine filler, shared with MSA يعني), **لِسَّا** (lissa, still/yet), **هَيْك** (hēk, like this/so).

Combined: **وِين رَايِح هَلَّق؟ بَدِّي رُوح عَ السُّوق** (wayn rāyiḥ halla'? biddī rūḥ ʿa s-sūq) — "Where are you going now? I want to go to the market."

Regional honesty: Levantine is a continuum — Beirut, Damascus, Amman, and Jerusalem each have their own vowels and words (Damascus keeps a more "classical" flavor in places; coastal Lebanon differs from the interior). And like Egyptians, Levantines slide toward MSA for formal topics without noticing. What unifies shāmī is the music: dropped vowels, softened consonants, and biddī/shū/halla' as its calling cards.
متى أستخدم الفصحى ومتى أستخدم العامية؟ أريد قاعدة عملية.

القاعدة العملية: **الفصحى للكتابة والرسميات، والعامية للحياة اليومية**.
(Al-qāʿida al-ʿamaliyya: al-fuṣḥā li-l-kitāba wa-r-rasmiyyāt, wa-l-ʿāmmiyya li-l-ḥayāh al-yawmiyya.)

**استخدم الفصحى عندما:**
(Istakhdim al-fuṣḥā ʿindamā:)

- تقرأ صحيفة أو كتابًا أو عقدًا (taqra'u ṣaḥīfa aw kitāban aw ʿaqdan — you read a newspaper, a book, a contract)
- تستمع إلى نشرة الأخبار (tastamiʿu ilā nashrat al-akhbār — you listen to the news bulletin)
- تتحدث في مقابلة رسمية أو محاضرة أو خطبة (tatḥaddathu fī muqābala rasmiyya aw muḥāḍara)
- تكتب رسالة رسمية أو مقالًا (taktubu risāla rasmiyya aw maqālan)

**استخدم العامية عندما:**
(Istakhdim al-ʿāmmiyya ʿindamā:)

- تتحدث مع الأصدقاء والعائلة (with friends and family)
- تشتري من السوق أو تركب سيارة أجرة (you shop in the market or ride a taxi)
- تمزح أو تحكي قصة شخصية (you joke or tell a personal story)
- تستمع إلى أغنية أو تشاهد مسلسلًا (you listen to a song or watch a series)

والحقيقة الوسطى: المتعلمون العرب يتحركون بين الطرفين باستمرار. المحاضر يشرح بالفصحى ويمزح بالعامية في الدرس نفسه. هذه ليست فوضى؛ اسمها **الازدواجية اللغوية**، وهي نظام العربية الطبيعي منذ قرون.
(Wa-l-ḥaqīqa al-wusṭā: al-mutaʿallimūn al-ʿarab yataḥarrakūna bayna ṭ-ṭarafayn bi-stimrār. Ismuhā: al-izdiwājiyya al-lughawiyya — diglossia.)

نصيحة للمتعلم الأجنبي: ابدأ بالفصحى لأنها تُفهم في كل مكان وتفتح لك القراءة، ثم تعلّم عامية البلد الذي ستعيش فيه أو تزوره. من يتكلم الفصحى فقط يُفهم دائمًا، لكنه يبدو كأنه يقرأ من كتاب؛ ومن يتعلم العامية أيضًا يصير ضيفًا لا سائحًا.
(Naṣīḥa: ibda' bi-l-fuṣḥā, thumma taʿallam ʿāmmiyyat al-balad alladhī sa-taʿīshu fīhi.)
Give me an honest learning strategy: MSA first, dialect first, or both at once?

Honest strategy, in order, with the reasoning exposed:

**Phase 1: MSA first — for the script, the roots, and the map.**
Start with Modern Standard Arabic for three to six months of foundations: the alphabet, the root system, core grammar, and survival vocabulary. Reasons: MSA is the only variety with abundant textbooks, courses, and dictionaries aimed at foreigners; it unlocks *reading* — signs, menus, news, messages — in every Arab country at once; and its grammar is the reference frame every dialect is described against. Trying to learn a dialect's "rules" without the MSA frame is like learning contractions before sentences.

**Phase 2: Add ONE dialect — the one where your life will happen.**
Choose by geography, not by prestige rankings: Egypt if you'll live in Cairo (with the bonus that Egyptian media made it understood region-wide), Levantine for Beirut/Damascus/Amman, Gulf for the Emirates/Saudi, Maghrebi only if the Maghreb is your destination (it's the most divergent and the hardest to bolt on later). Learn it *orally* — conversation, series, songs — on top of your MSA reading.

**Phase 3: Let them specialize.**
The mature division of labor in your own head should mirror the Arab world's: read and write MSA; talk dialect; understand that educated speech lives on a slope between them. Trying to speak *pure* MSA socially forever is the one real mistake — you'll be understood and subtly kept at arm's length, a walking newspaper.

**What not to do:**
- Don't learn two dialects at once as a beginner; they'll cross-wire (Egyptian ʿāyiz in a Beirut sentence marks you as a tourist of both).
- Don't skip the script for transliteration-only dialect courses; illiterate fluency caps out fast.
- Don't apologize for MSA pronunciation in dialect land. Arabs switch *toward* MSA to meet foreigners halfway; meet them on the slope.

Realistic timeline with steady work: script and roots in a month, survival MSA conversation in six, comfortable reading in a year or two, dialect warmth arriving steadily from month four. Arabic is a long language — but it starts paying rent (signs read, greetings returned, roots guessed) in the first fortnight.
I've heard Gulf Arabic and Maghrebi Arabic are the extremes. What's different about each?

They are the two ends of the dialect map — Gulf speech stays relatively close to classical patterns in some ways while innovating in others, and Maghrebi is famously the hardest for other Arabs to follow. Careful, honest sketches:

**Gulf (خليجي, khalījī — Saudi, UAE, Kuwait, Qatar, Bahrain, Oman):**
- **چ (ch) sound**: in Kuwaiti, Iraqi, and parts of the Gulf, ك becomes "ch" in many words — كَيْف (kayf, how) → **چيف** (chēf); كبير (kabīr) → **چبير** (chibīr) in Iraqi especially. The letter چ isn't in the MSA alphabet; it's borrowed for writing this sound.
- **ج often pronounced "y"** in coastal Gulf: جَدِيد (jadīd) → **يديد** (yidīd, new) in Emirati/Bahraini speech.
- **Vocabulary**: **وَايِد** (wāyid, "very/much"), **شلونك** (shlōnak, "how are you" — literally "what's your color"), **أَبِي** (abī, "I want," alongside أبغى abghā in Saudi).
- Bedouin features survive strongly: the Gulf kept some classical sounds (like ق as "g" in Bedouin varieties: قال → gāl) that city dialects elsewhere dropped.

**Maghrebi (دارجة, dārija — Morocco, Algeria, Tunisia; Libya bridges east):**
- **Vowel reduction**: short vowels vanish into clusters — MSA كَتَبَ (kataba) → Moroccan **كتب** (kteb). Whole syllables collapse; to eastern ears it sounds like the vowels were rationed.
- **First-person verbs take n-…**: "I write" is **نكتب** (nikteb) — the n- that means "we" elsewhere in Arabic means "I" here, a genuinely disorienting flip for visitors.
- **French everywhere**: centuries of contact stocked dārija with French loans — **طوموبيل** (ṭūmūbīl, car, from *automobile*), **كوزينة** (kūzīna, kitchen, from *cuisine*) — plus Spanish traces in northern Morocco and Amazigh (Berber) substrate throughout.
- **Negation and questions**: **ما…ش** (ma…sh) like Egypt, but **علاش** (ʿlāsh, "why") and **بزاف** (bizzāf, "a lot/very") mark Morocco instantly.

The honesty clause: these are regional generalizations over millions of speakers; a Casablancan and a rural Moroccan differ plenty, and educated Maghrebis code-switch into French and MSA constantly — which is also your bridge: in the Maghreb, MSA (and often French) is how an eastern-trained learner gets understood while the ear adjusts. The reputation "Maghrebi is hardest" is really "Maghrebi is farthest from the MSA anchor" — distance, not difficulty of character.
Do educated Arabs really mix MSA and dialect in the same conversation? What does that sound like?

Constantly — and it has a name: **Educated Spoken Arabic**, the sliding register of lectures, talk shows, offices, and serious conversation among friends. Nobody switches cleanly; speakers move along a slope, rising toward MSA for weight and dropping into dialect for warmth, humor, and asides — often mid-sentence.

A composed but realistic example — a professor opening a talk:

**«الْيَوْمَ سَنَتَحَدَّثُ عَنْ مُشْكِلَةِ الْمِيَاهِ فِي الْمِنْطَقَةِ. يَعْنِي، الْمَوْضُوع مِش سَهْل، بَسّ لَازِم نِفْهَمُه كُوَيِّس.»**
"Today we will discuss (MSA: al-yawma sa-nataḥaddathu ʿan mushkilati l-miyāhi fī l-minṭaqa) the water problem in the region. I mean (yaʿnī — the bridge word), the topic isn't easy (dialect: mish sahl), but we have to understand it well (lāzim nifhamu kuwayyis — Egyptian-flavored dialect)."

Watch the machinery:

1. **The topic sentence is MSA** — formal vocabulary (مشكلة المياه، المنطقة), full case endings half-pronounced, the sa- future.
2. **The connective tissue is dialect** — يعني (yaʿnī, "meaning/I mean") is the universal hinge; it exists in MSA but lives as everyone's filler.
3. **The human verdict is dialect** — mish (not), lāzim (must), kuwayyis (well/good): opinions, jokes, and emotions come out in the mother tongue.
4. **Quotations rise**: citing a law, a verse, a statistic, or a headline pulls the speaker up-register automatically; telling what his grandmother said about it drops him back down.

The same slope runs in reverse at home: a father helping with homework reads the textbook aloud in MSA, then explains it in dialect — the explanation is where understanding happens, so the explanation wears the home language.

For you as a learner, this is liberating news: **the mixed register is the target, not a failure mode.** Arabs will not grade your speech for purity. They'll do what they do with each other — ride the slope with you, rising when you rise, dropping when you drop. Your job is range, not allegiance.
اشرح لي ببساطة: ما الفرق بين الفصحى والعامية؟

الفرق ببساطة: **الفصحى لغة الكتابة والرسميات، والعامية لغة البيت والشارع**.
(Al-farq bi-basāṭa: al-fuṣḥā lughat al-kitāba wa-r-rasmiyyāt, wa-l-ʿāmmiyya lughat al-bayt wa-sh-shāriʿ.)

**الفصحى** (al-fuṣḥā): هي لغة القرآن والكتب والصحف ونشرات الأخبار. لا يتكلمها أحد لغةً أمًّا في البيت؛ يتعلمها الأطفال في المدرسة. وهي واحدة من المحيط إلى الخليج: المغربي والمصري والعراقي يقرؤون الصحيفة نفسها.
(Hiya lughat al-Qur'ān wa-l-kutub wa-ṣ-ṣuḥuf. Lā yatakallamuhā aḥad lughatan umman fī l-bayt; yataʿallamuhā l-aṭfāl fī l-madrasa.)

**العامية** (al-ʿāmmiyya): هي ما يتكلمه الناس فعلًا كل يوم، وتختلف من بلد إلى بلد: مصرية، شامية، خليجية، مغربية. بها النكات والأغاني والمسلسلات وأحاديث السوق.
(Hiya mā yatakallamuhu n-nās fiʿlan kulla yawm, wa-takhtalifu min balad ilā balad.)

مثال واحد يوضح كل شيء — «أريد أن أذهب الآن»:
(Mithāl wāḥid yuwaḍḍiḥu kull shay' — "urīdu an adhhaba l-ān":)

- فصحى: **أُرِيدُ أَنْ أَذْهَبَ الْآنَ** (urīdu an adhhaba l-ān)
