- مصرية: **عَايِز أَرُوح دِلْوَقْتِي** (ʿāyiz arūḥ dilwa'ti)
- شامية: **بَدِّي رُوح هَلَّق** (biddī rūḥ halla')

ولا تظن أن العامية «عربية مكسورة»؛ هي نظام كامل بقواعدها، والفصحى والعامية أختان من أصل واحد، ولكل واحدة مكانتها.
(Wa-lā taẓunna anna l-ʿāmmiyya "ʿarabiyya maksūra"; hiya niẓām kāmil bi-qawāʿidihā.)

إذا تعلمت الفصحى أولًا، فأنت تبني الأساس الذي تُقاس عليه العاميات كلها.
(Idhā taʿallamta l-fuṣḥā awwalan, fa-anta tabnī l-asās alladhī tuqāsu ʿalayhi l-ʿāmmiyyāt kulluhā.)
I photographed a shop sign in Amman: مخبز النور — مفتوح من الساعة الثامنة صباحا حتى العاشرة مساء. Read it with me.

Let's read your sign the way a learner should — sign first, then the machinery:

**مَخْبَزُ النُّورِ**
Makhbazu n-Nūr
"The Bakery of Light" (Nūr is also a common name — this may be Mr. Nour's bakery; the sign works either way.)

- **مَخْبَز** (makhbaz) — the ma- place pattern on the root خ ب ز (kh-b-z, bread/baking): "place of baking" = bakery. You guessed this family in the مطعم lesson.
- **النُّور** (an-nūr) — "the light." ن is a sun letter, so ال assimilates: an-nūr, with shadda on the ن. Written مخبز النور, read makhbazu **n**-nūr.

**مَفْتُوحٌ مِنَ السَّاعَةِ الثَّامِنَةِ صَبَاحًا حَتَّى الْعَاشِرَةِ مَسَاءً**
maftūḥun min as-sāʿati th-thāminati ṣabāḥan ḥattā l-ʿāshirati masā'an
"Open from eight o'clock in the morning until ten in the evening."

- **مَفْتُوح** (maftūḥ) — "open," the passive participle of فَتَحَ (fataḥa, to open): mafʿūl pattern, "the opened thing."
- **السَّاعَة الثَّامِنَة** (as-sāʿa ath-thāmina) — "the eighth hour" = 8 o'clock; feminine ordinal agreeing with ساعة (also a sun-letter assimilation: as-sāʿa, th-thāmina — س and ث are both sun letters).
- **صَبَاحًا / مَسَاءً** (ṣabāḥan / masā'an) — "in the morning / in the evening," the -an adverbial endings doing the work of AM/PM.
- **حَتَّى** (ḥattā) — "until."

Your sign, fully read, told you: the shop's name, its trade, and its hours — with four sun-letter assimilations, a place-pattern noun, a passive participle, and two ordinal numbers, all in eleven words. Street Arabic is dense like this everywhere, which is why reading signs is the best homework in the language: short, real, and proud of their grammar.
News headlines in Arabic look like sentence fragments. Here's one: وزير التعليم يفتتح مدرسة جديدة في القاهرة. Break down how headlines work.

Your headline: **وَزِيرُ التَّعْلِيمِ يَفْتَتِحُ مَدْرَسَةً جَدِيدَةً فِي الْقَاهِرَةِ**
wazīru t-taʿlīmi yaftatiḥu madrasatan jadīdatan fī l-Qāhira
"The Minister of Education inaugurates a new school in Cairo."

Word by word:

- **وَزِيرُ التَّعْلِيمِ** (wazīru t-taʿlīm) — an iḍāfa: "minister-of education" = the Education Minister. (تعليم taʿlīm is the verbal noun of Form II علّم, "teaching" — the ministry's name is a root-family word.)
- **يَفْتَتِحُ** (yaftatiḥu) — "inaugurates/opens." Form VIII of ف ت ح (opening): the -ta- infix after the first root letter marks it. Note the tense: present in form, but headlines use the present for **just-completed events** — the opening happened, the headline reports it in the vivid present, exactly like English "Minister opens school."
- **مَدْرَسَةً جَدِيدَةً** (madrasatan jadīdatan) — "a new school," both words carrying -an: indefinite accusative object, adjective marching in step.
- **فِي الْقَاهِرَةِ** (fī l-Qāhira) — "in Cairo" — a proper name with ال built in.

Now the headline style rules you've been sensing:

1. **Short vowels vanish entirely** — headlines are the least voweled Arabic in print; you read وزير التعليم from consonants and context, as natives do.
2. **Verbless headlines are common**: «مَدْرَسَةٌ جَدِيدَةٌ فِي الْقَاهِرَةِ» ("New school in Cairo") or the pure announcement «وَفَاةُ…» (wafātu…, "Death of…") — the nominal fragment is a complete headline.
3. **The present tense reports the recent past** (as above), and سَـ/سَوْفَ mark the genuinely future story: «سَيَفْتَتِحُ…» — "will inaugurate."
4. **Nouns stack in iḍāfa chains** to compress: «مُدِيرُ عَامِّ شَرِكَةِ…» — headlines are iḍāfa's natural habitat.

Practice protocol: read the headline, predict the story, then read the first paragraph and check. Headlines are the cheapest daily reading in Arabic — one line, whole grammar.
A friend texted me: ازيك يا أحمد، عامل ايه؟ أنا في الطريق وهكون عندك كمان عشر دقايق — and then switched to Latin letters: '3ayez 7aga min barra?' Decode all of it.

Your friend wrote you a perfect specimen of real digital Arabic — Egyptian dialect in Arabic script, then the same dialect in **Arabizi**. Decoding:

**Part 1 (Arabic script):**
**ازيك يا أحمد، عامل ايه؟ أنا في الطريق وهكون عندك كمان عشر دقايق**
izzayyak yā Aḥmad, ʿāmil ēh? ana fī aṭ-ṭarī', wa-hakūn ʿandak kamān ʿashar da'āyi'
"How are you, Ahmad? How's it going? I'm on the way and I'll be at your place in ten more minutes."

- **ازيك** (izzayyak) — Egyptian "how are you (m.)"
- **عامل ايه** (ʿāmil ēh) — literally "doing what?" = "how are you / what's up" — pure Egypt.
- **في الطريق** (fī aṭ-ṭarī') — "on the road/on my way" (ط is a sun letter: aṭ-ṭarī').
- **هكون عندك** (hakūn ʿandak) — "I will be at your place" — ha- future prefix glued on.
- **كمان عشر دقايق** (kamān ʿashar da'āyi') — "in ten more minutes" (كمان kamān = "also/more"; دقايق da'āyi' = minutes, dialect plural of دقيقة).

**Part 2 (Arabizi / Franco-Arabic):**
**"3ayez 7aga min barra?"** = **عايز حاجة من برة؟** (ʿāyiz ḥāga min barra?) — "Do you want anything from outside?"

Arabizi writes Arabic sounds with Latin letters plus **digits for the letters Latin lacks**:

- **3 = ع** (ʿayn — the digit looks like a reversed ع)
- **7 = ح** (ḥā' — a stylized ح)
- **5 = خ** (khā' — as in "5abar" = خبر, news)
- **2 = ء/ق** in some regions (hamza; in Egypt often the ق-turned-hamza: "2albi" = قلبي, my heart)
- **8 = غ** (ghayn) in some conventions

Why does Arabizi exist? Legacy keyboards and phones without Arabic input — and today, habit and speed among the young. It is informal-only: nobody writes a contract or a headline in it. But chats mix scripts mid-sentence exactly as your friend did, and reading Arabizi is mostly learning the digit-letters: 3, 7, 5 carry almost all of it.

Your reply, to keep the register: **لا، شكرا يا صاحبي، مستنيك** (lā, shukran yā ṣāḥbī, mistannīk) — "No thanks, man, I'm waiting for you."
I'm staring at a menu in Beirut. The sections say المقبلات and المشويات and there are words like حمص and متبل and فتوش. Walk me through it.

You're holding a standard Levantine menu. Let's read your section:

**الْمُقَبِّلَات** (al-muqabbilāt) — "the appetizers/starters." The word is a participle: "the things that make you accept (the meal)" — المقبلات is the opening act of every Levantine table.

- **حُمُّص** (ḥummuṣ) — hummus. (The word also means "chickpeas" themselves — the dish is named for its bean.)
- **مُتَبَّل** (mutabbal) — in Lebanon usually **eggplant** mashed with tahini (baba ghanoush's close cousin; mutabbal literally means "seasoned/spiced"). Expect the smoky eggplant dip.
- **سَلَطَةُ فَتُّوش** (salaṭat fattūsh) — fattoush: the chopped salad with toasted pita chips and sumac. فتوش from فَتَّ (fatta, to crumble/break bread) — the name describes the broken bread in it.

**الْمَشْوِيَّات** (al-mashwiyyāt) — "the grilled things" — from شَوَى (shawā, to grill). The section to find **مَشَاوِي مُشَكَّلَة** (mashāwī mushakkala, mixed grill) — مشكلة here means "assorted/formed (varied)," not "problem"! (Same spelling, different word: مُشْكِلَة mushkila is "problem"; مُشَكَّلَة mushakkala is "assorted." Vowels matter; context shouts.)

More sections and dishes you'll meet:

- **الشُّورَبَات** (ash-shūrabāt) — soups; **شُورَبَةُ عَدَس** (shūrabat ʿadas) — lentil soup.
- **الْحَلَوِيَّات** (al-ḥalawiyyāt) — desserts; **كُنَافَة** (kunāfa) — the shredded-pastry cheese dessert, ordered **نَاعِمَة** (nāʿima, fine) or **خَشِنَة** (khashina, coarse) in Lebanon.
- **الْمَشْرُوبَات** (al-mashrūbāt) — drinks; **جَلَّاب** (jallāb) — the Levantine date-syrup drink with pine nuts.

Ordering line that covers the table: **بَدْنَا حُمُّص وَمُتَبَّل وَمَشَاوِي مُشَكَّلَة، مِنْ فَضْلِك** (baddnā ḥummuṣ wa-mutabbal wa-mashāwī mushakkala, min faḍlik) — "We'd like (Levantine: baddnā, 'we want') hummus, mutabbal, and the mixed grill, please." Menus are the friendliest Arabic reading there is: short lines, no verbs, and dinner at the end.
There's a nameplate on an office door: د. أحمد الشريف. And I keep seeing family names like النجار and الحداد. Teach me to read Arabic names.

Your nameplate first: **د. أَحْمَد الشَّرِيف** — "Dr. Aḥmad ash-Sharīf." The د. is the standard abbreviation for دكتور (duktūr). الشريف (ash-Sharīf) is a family name meaning "the noble/honorable" — and notice it demonstrates the sun-letter rule: ش is a sun letter, so ال is pronounced ash-, never al-.

Arabic names traditionally stack in layers, and reading the layers tells you about the person:

1. **The given name** (الاسم): أحمد، محمد، فاطمة، مريم… Many are root-words: **أَحْمَد** (Aḥmad, "most praiseworthy," root ḥ-m-d), **كَرِيم** (Karīm, "generous"), **سَلْمَى** (Salmā, "safe/sound," root s-l-m).
2. **The family name / nisba** — often one of three kinds:
   - **Occupational**: **النَّجَّار** (an-najjār, "the carpenter"), **الْحَدَّاد** (al-ḥaddād, "the blacksmith"), **الْخَيَّاط** (al-khayyāṭ, "the tailor"), **الصَّيَّاد** (aṣ-ṣayyād, "the fisherman/hunter") — the faʿʿāl profession pattern wearing a ال. Ancestors' trades became surnames, exactly as with English Smith and Baker.
   - **Place nisba** with the ـي (-ī) ending: **الْمِصْرِي** (al-Miṣrī, "the Egyptian"), **الْحَلَبِي** (al-Ḥalabī, "the Aleppan"), **الْبَغْدَادِي** (al-Baghdādī).
   - **Descriptive/honorific**: الشريف (the noble), **الْكَبِير** (al-kabīr, "the elder/great").
3. **بن / ابن** (ibn, "son of") chains in formal full names: أحمد بن محمد — "Ahmad son of Muḥammad"; بنت (bint) for daughters. Gulf and formal documents keep long chains; daily life uses first + family.
4. **The kunya**: **أَبُو** (abū, "father of") + eldest child or a trait — أبو أحمد is how colleagues may actually address Dr. ash-Sharīf; أُمّ (umm, "mother of") for women. It's an honorific of respect and warmth, used even for people whose "child" is metaphorical (أبو الهول, Abū l-Hawl — "Father of Terror," the Sphinx's Arabic name!).

Pronunciation rule for the door: apply sun/moon to every ال — **النجار** is an-najjār (ن sun), **الحداد** is al-ḥaddād (ح moon). Read the name aloud correctly once, and you've shown the office more respect than a perfect bow.
Here's my first real Arabic paragraph: يقع بيتي في حي قديم في القاهرة. في الصباح أشرب القهوة في الشرفة وأشاهد الشارع. Read it slowly with me — every mechanism.

A beautiful first paragraph — a home, a morning, coffee. Let's go word by word; nearly every lesson you've learned is hiding in these two sentences.

**يَقَعُ بَيْتِي فِي حَيٍّ قَدِيمٍ فِي الْقَاهِرَةِ**
yaqaʿu baytī fī ḥayyin qadīmin fī l-Qāhirati
"My house is located in an old neighborhood in Cairo."

- **يَقَعُ** (yaqaʿu) — "is located/falls." Present tense, ya- prefix, root **و ق ع** (w-q-ʿ) — a first-weak verb: the و drops in the present (compare وَقَعَ waqaʿa, "he fell," where it shows). Arabic says a house "falls" in a district.
- **بَيْتِي** (baytī) — "my house": noun + possessive suffix ـي. No separate word for "my."
- **حَيٍّ** (ḥayyin) — "neighborhood/district" — and also "alive" (same word: a district is the living quarter). The shadda on ي and the tanwīn -in (genitive after fī) are both visible in careful writing.
- **قَدِيمٍ** (qadīmin) — "old," adjective after its noun, matching genitive -in. Indefinite phrase: "**an** old neighborhood."

**فِي الصَّبَاحِ أَشْرَبُ الْقَهْوَةَ فِي الشُّرْفَةِ وَأُشَاهِدُ الشَّارِعَ**
fī ṣ-ṣabāḥi ashrabu l-qahwata fī sh-shurfati wa-ushāhidu sh-shāriʿa
"In the morning I drink coffee on the balcony and watch the street."

- **فِي الصَّبَاحِ** — ص is a sun letter: fī **ṣ**-ṣabāḥ. Your third assimilation of the paragraph (also الشُّرْفَة ash-shurfa and الشَّارِع ash-shāriʿ — ش is a sun letter too). The paragraph is quietly drilling you.
- **أَشْرَبُ** (ashrabu) — "I drink": a- prefix, root ش ر ب. Its object **الْقَهْوَةَ** (al-qahwata) keeps al- — ق is a moon letter — and ends in -a, the accusative.
- **الشُّرْفَة** (ash-shurfa) — "the balcony." Root ش ر ف (honor/overlooking) — a balcony is the house's high, overlooking place; شريف (sharīf, "noble") is its cousin. Roots reward you mid-paragraph.
- **أُشَاهِدُ** (ushāhidu) — "I watch/observe": **Form III** of ش ه د (witnessing) — the long ā after the first root letter is Form III's signature, "engaging with" the scene.
- **الشَّارِعَ** (ash-shāriʿa) — "the street," accusative -a again, object of watching.

Count what the paragraph made you use: a weak verb, a possessive suffix, tanwīn, three sun-letter assimilations against one moon letter, two accusative objects, and a Form III verb. That is not a beginner text *about* Arabic — that is Arabic, at full density, in two lines. Read it aloud three times; the fourth time, it reads itself.
أرى كلمات متكررة على اللافتات في الشوارع العربية: ممنوع، مدخل، مخرج، للبيع. ماذا تعني؟

هذه كلمات اللافتات الأساسية، وستقرؤها كل يوم في أي مدينة عربية.
(Hādhihi kalimāt al-lāfitāt al-asāsiyya.)

- **مَمْنُوعُ الْوُقُوفِ** (mamnūʿu l-wuqūf — No parking): ممنوع تعني «forbidden»، وتأتي معها كلمات كثيرة: **ممنوع التدخين** (mamnūʿ at-tadkhīn — no smoking)، **ممنوع الدخول** (mamnūʿ ad-dukhūl — no entry).
- **مَدْخَل** (madkhal — entrance): من الجذر د خ ل، وعلى وزن «مَفْعَل» أي مكان الدخول.
- **مَخْرَج** (makhraj — exit): من الجذر خ ر ج، نفس الوزن. و**مخرج طوارئ** (makhraj ṭawāri' — emergency exit).
- **اِدْفَع** (idfaʿ — push) و**اِسْحَب** (isḥab — pull): على الأبواب الزجاجية في كل مكان.
- **لِلْبَيْعِ** (li-l-bayʿ — for sale): على المحلات والسيارات والبيوت. وعكسها: **لِلْإِيجَارِ** (li-l-ījār — for rent).
- **اِحْذَر** (iḥdhar — caution/beware): على لافتات الخطر.
- **مَفْتُوح / مُغْلَق** (maftūḥ / mughlaq — open / closed): على باب كل محل.
- **خُذْ رَقْمًا وَانْتَظِرْ** (khudh raqman wa-ntaẓir — take a number and wait): في البنوك والمؤسسات.

لاحظ أن أكثر هذه الكلمات على أوزان تعرفها: مدخل ومخرج على وزن المكان (مَفْعَل)، وممنوع ومفتوح على وزن المفعول (مَفْعُول). اللافتات درس قواعد مجاني في الشارع.
(Lāḥiẓ anna akthar hādhihi l-kalimāt ʿalā awzān taʿrifuhā: madkhal wa-makhraj ʿalā wazn al-makān, wa-mamnūʿ wa-maftūḥ ʿalā wazn al-mafʿūl.)

تدريب: في مشوارك القادم، اقرأ كل لافتة بصوت عالٍ، وخمّن معناها من الجذر قبل أن تترجمها.
(Tadrīb: fī mishwārik al-qādim, iqra' kull lāfita bi-ṣawt ʿālin, wa-khammin maʿnāhā min al-jadhr.)
An Egyptian friend sent me a photo of a receipt: فاتورة — ٢ كجم أرز، ١ لتر حليب، ٣ علب عصير، المجموع ٤٥ جنيها، شامل الضريبة. Read it for me.

Your receipt, line by line:

**فَاتُورَة** (fātūra) — "invoice/receipt." A loanword (from Italian *fattura* via trade) that Arabic fully adopted — receipts across the region are فواتير (fawātīr, its broken plural).

**٢ كجم أَرْز** (2 kg urz) — "2 kg rice." The digit is Eastern Arabic-Indic **٢** (2). كجم is the written abbreviation of كيلوغرام (kīlūghrām). أَرْز (urz) — rice; in Egyptian speech it's رُزّ (ruzz).

**١ لِتْر حَلِيب** (1 litr ḥalīb) — "1 liter of milk." لتر is another naturalized loan. حليب (ḥalīb) is MSA "milk" — in Egypt fresh milk is usually **لَبَن** (laban) on receipts and in shops, while حليب is understood and used for packaged/long-life milk (and in the Levant/Gulf ḥalīb is the everyday word). Regional vocabulary reaches all the way into the grocery list.

**٣ عُلَب عَصِير** (3 ʿulab ʿaṣīr) — "3 packs/cartons of juice." عُلَب is the plural of عُلْبَة (ʿulba, a small box/pack) — and notice: after the number 3, Egyptian commercial writing uses the plural noun loosely, where classical grammar wants the polarity construction (ثلاث علبٍ). Real receipts bend formal rules; read for the items and quantities, not for case endings.

**الْمَجْمُوع: ٤٥ جُنَيْهًا** (al-majmūʿ: 45 junayhan) — "Total: 45 pounds." المجموع is literally "the gathered (amount)." The noun after 45 keeps its formal singular accusative form جُنَيْهًا (junayhan) — even on a casual receipt, the 11–99 rule leaves its fingerprint in writing.

**شَامِل الضَّرِيبَة** (shāmil aḍ-ḍarība) — "including tax" (literally "inclusive of the tax"). ضَرِيبَة (ḍarība) is tax; شَامِل (shāmil) means "comprehensive/including."

What the receipt teaches beyond its items: Eastern digits in daily use, loanwords naturalized (فاتورة، لتر), MSA and dialect vocabulary side by side (حليب on paper, لبن in the Cairo shop), and formal grammar surviving in exactly one fossil — that جُنَيْهًا. A grocery receipt is a tiny dialect-MSA treaty, printed on thermal paper.
I want to read the weather forecast in Arabic. Today's says: درجات الحرارة غدا: العظمى ٣٢ والصغرى ٢١، والرياح خفيفة، والجو مشمس. Help me through it.

Your forecast, fully read:

**دَرَجَاتُ الْحَرَارَةِ غَدًا**
darajātu l-ḥarārati ghadan
"Temperatures (literally 'degrees of heat') tomorrow." درجات الحرارة is the fixed phrase for the temperature forecast — an iḍāfa chain: degrees-of the-heat.

**الْعُظْمَى ٣٢ وَالصُّغْرَى ٢١**
al-ʿuẓmā 32 wa-ṣ-ṣughrā 21
"The high (is) 32 and the low 21."

- **الْعُظْمَى** (al-ʿuẓmā) — "the greatest (fem.)" — the elative of عَظِيم (ʿaẓīm, great), in its feminine form because it describes دَرَجَة (daraja, a degree, fem.). The high temperature.
- **الصُّغْرَى** (aṣ-ṣughrā) — "the smallest (fem.)" — the low. ص is a sun letter: a**ṣ**-ṣughrā.
- The digits are Eastern: **٣٢** = 32, **٢١** = 21. (Degrees Celsius, the region's standard.)

**وَالرِّيَاحُ خَفِيفَةٌ**
wa-r-riyāḥu khafīfatun
"And the winds (are) light." — رِيَاح (riyāḥ) is the plural of رِيح (rīḥ, wind), treated as feminine singular for agreement — خَفِيفَة (khafīfa, light) — your non-human plural rule, live on the weather page.

**وَالْجَوُّ مُشْمِسٌ**
wa-l-jawwu mushmisun
"And the weather (is) sunny." — جَوّ (jaww) is the everyday word for weather/atmosphere; مُشْمِس (mushmis) is a participle from أَشْمَسَ (ashmasa, "to be sunny," Form IV of the ش م س sun root) — "sun-shining."

The forecast phrase bank, for tomorrow's reading: **غَائِم جُزْئِيًّا** (ghā'im juz'iyyan, partly cloudy)، **أَمْطَار خَفِيفَة** (amṭār khafīfa, light rain)، **رُطُوبَة عَالِيَة** (ruṭūba ʿāliya, high humidity)، **عَاصِفَة رَمْلِيَّة** (ʿāṣifa ramliyya, sandstorm — a Gulf/region staple). Weather Arabic is formulaic by design: ten phrases and you can read the sky in any Arab newspaper.
اقرأ معي هذه الجملة واشرحها كلمة كلمة: «العلم نور والجهل ظلام».

جملة قصيرة وعميقة، وهي مثال كامل على الجملة الاسمية.
(Jumla qaṣīra wa-ʿamīqa, wa-hiya mithāl kāmil ʿalā l-jumla al-ismiyya.)

**الْعِلْمُ نُورٌ**
al-ʿilmu nūrun
"Knowledge is light."

- **الْعِلْمُ** (al-ʿilm): المبتدأ — المعرفة والدراسة. جذره **ع ل م**، نفس جذر **عالِم** (ʿālim — scholar) و**مَعْلُومَات** (maʿlūmāt — information) و**تَعْلِيم** (taʿlīm — education).
- **نُورٌ** (nūr): الخبر — الضوء. جذره **ن و ر**، ومنه **مَنَارَة** (manāra — lighthouse) و**مُنِير** (munīr — shining) و**أَنَارَ** (anāra — he lit up).

لاحظ: لا توجد كلمة بمعنى «is» — الجملة الاسمية تضع المبتدأ والخبر جنبًا إلى جنب.
(Lāḥiẓ: lā tūjadu kalima bi-maʿnā "is" — al-jumla al-ismiyya taḍaʿu l-mubtada' wa-l-khabar janban ilā janb.)

**وَالْجَهْلُ ظَلَامٌ**
wa-l-jahlu ẓalāmun
"And ignorance is darkness."

- **الْجَهْلُ** (al-jahl): ضد العلم — جذره **ج ه ل**، ومنه **جَاهِل** (jāhil — ignorant).
- **ظَلَامٌ** (ẓalām): عكس النور — من الجذر **ظ ل م**، ومنه **ظُلْم** (ẓulm — injustice)؛ فالظلم في العربية «ظلام» في المعاملة، والكلمتان أختان.

والجملتان معًا صورة بلاغية: العلم يُقابَل بالجهل، والنور بالظلام — وهذا التقابل اسمه **الطباق** في البلاغة العربية.
(Wa-l-jumlatān maʿan ṣūra balāghiyya: hādhā at-taqābul ismuhu aṭ-ṭibāq fī l-balāgha al-ʿarabiyya.)

تدرّب: اصنع جملة على نفس الوزن: **الكتاب صديق** (al-kitābu ṣadīq — the book is a friend).
(Tadarrab: iṣnaʿ jumla ʿalā nafs al-wazn.)
